    Item 28(f) argued: generation is 57 % of the mean round trip, therefore generation is where the ~1,480 ms of scatter lives, therefore removing it removes the scatter. **The middle step does not follow, and this run measures why: SD(`afterFirst`) is 314 and 408 ms.** Generation is a large share of the **mean** and a negligible share of the **variance**. **A share of the mean is not a share of the variance**, and item 28(f) — in a revision whose entire subject was reading one statistic as though it were another — treated them as the same quantity. **This document has now made that class of error three times** (item 25's r², item 28(a)'s r², and here), which is why it is recorded as a class rather than as an incident.

    **(d) The estimator that does help is the one nobody proposed, and it was already being recorded.** Time to **response headers** — before any token, and therefore genuinely free of generation:

    | | SD, arm A | SD, arm B | corr with total |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | `headers` | **2,203 ms** | **1,973 ms** | 0.63 / 0.78 |
    | `TTFT` | 2,989 ms | 3,056 ms | **0.995 / 0.991** |
    | `total` | 2,878 ms | 2,959 ms | — |

    **~25–33 % lower SD, and a correlation that shows it is a different measurement rather than a shifted copy.** It costs nothing — the probe timestamps it on the way past. **The lesson generalises past this run: the useful cut point was one event earlier than the one that had a name.**

    **(e) The doctrine comparison is null on every estimator, and on the best one the sign is backwards.** Arm A minus arm B, the prefix delta being **2,202 cached tokens**:

    | Estimator | A − B | 95 % interval | |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | `headers` | **−103 ms** | [−940, +733] | includes zero |
    | `TTFT` | +549 ms | [−660, +1,758] | includes zero |
    | `total` | +454 ms | [−714, +1,621] | includes zero |

    **This is the null result the fifth grant pre-accepted, and it is reported as an outcome rather than as a failed attempt.** The best estimator resolves anything above **837 ms** (against total's 1,168 ms — the 28 % improvement is real but did not change the verdict), and it puts the cost of 2,202 cached prefix tokens at **−103 ms**, with the *short*-doctrine arm marginally **slower**. That is the **second** time a prefix reduction has failed to move latency in the predicted direction: v1.8.5 cut ~1,617 cached tokens and moved p50 down 16 % while moving p95 **up** 54 %. Two independent runs, one of them with a purpose-built instrument, and no consistent prefix effect in either.

    **(f) And the number that actually closes C2 was never the one being argued about.** *(Rescoped v1.8.16 — §Corrections item 33(d). Both arms of this run are **`claude-sonnet-5`**; §Success metrics' ≤ 2.5 s row is **Haiku's**. The verdict stands and the reason is narrowed to the model that produced it.)*

    > **On `claude-sonnet-5`, time to response headers — before one token has been generated — has a mean of 3,157 ms and a p95 of 6,917 ms on arm A, and 3,260 / 7,357 ms on arm B.**

    **On that model the fixed term alone exceeds the total-latency target, by 26 % at the mean and by 176 % at p95.** No reduction in prompt size, output length, or schema can bring a 2.5 s p95 out of a path whose pre-generation phase is already 6.9 s at p95. **The target was set in v1.2 against no hosted measurement of any kind, and on `claude-sonnet-5` it was never achievable** — which is a different and more useful finding than "the p95 is 4,615 ms and we do not know why."

    **What this does NOT establish, and the limit is a model boundary rather than a statistical one.** **Haiku's fixed term has never been measured.** Item 24 established that tokenization is model-specific; item 28 is a sustained argument about not reading one model's data as another's; and the two differ materially here — Sonnet's mean round trip is 7,393 ms against Haiku's measured p95 of 4,615 ms, so Sonnet's *headers* alone nearly reach Haiku's whole *total*. If Haiku's fixed term were ≈1,800 ms the latency row would still read **MISSED**, but the cause this subsection closes on would be the wrong one. **Carried as C10**, answerable for ≈$0.10 from the archived request bodies whenever a grant exists. **Not requested here.**

    **What follows, and what does not.** The remedy is not prompt-side: it is a different model, a different target, or accepting the miss — and **the 20 s cadence already accepts it**, absorbing p99 with room to spare, which is why no run in any phase has been degraded by this. **§Success metrics' latency row is left unchanged and still reads MISSED.** Moving a target to match a measurement is the one thing this document has refused since v1.3, and it is not going to start here. **C2 closes with a cause rather than a remedy.**

    **(g) Cost, including the overrun.** 109 requests ≈ **$0.84**, against **≈$0.50** estimated in the fifth grant — **+68 %**. Thirteen of those requests were instrument development, and they were not free: the first smoke run measured two samples pinned at ~30,500 ms that turned out to be .NET's `Expect100Continue` handshake, not the service. **That is a probe measuring its own client stack and reporting it as latency**, caught only because 30,498 and 30,501 ms are not what variance looks like. Running total **≈$2.16 of $5**.

30. **C3's quality arm, pre-registered: what n=120 can and cannot resolve, and the decision rule, both written down before the run.** *(v1.8.13 — no request has been made at the time of this entry. The fifth grant (v1.8.11) conditions this run on exactly that ordering.)*

    **Why this is an item and not a paragraph in the results.** Every prior arm in this project was designed, run, and *then* assessed for whether it could have detected anything — and twice the answer was no (the C2 doctrine arms, §Corrections item 28(d); the TTFT instrument, item 29(c)). **A power statement written after a null result is indistinguishable from an excuse.** This one is written first so that it cannot become one.

    **(a) The change under test.** `PromptRenderer::build` renders the order schema into the prefix as prose; `ClaudeLlmClient` *also* sends it structurally as `output_config.format.schema`. §Corrections item 22 measured the duplication at **~71 % of the cached prefix**, and v1.8.5 confirmed the cost half — cutting the prefix saved **12 %** per four-ship-hour. **What has never been measured is what the prose copy is worth.** The arm removes exactly that block and nothing else, with structured outputs left **on**, because the premise of the proposed change is that the structural copy does the constraining.

    **(b) What n=120 per arm can resolve, exactly.** The metric is acceptance rate, the same one §Success metrics gates at **≥ 95 %**. Exact (Clopper–Pearson) one-sided 95 % lower bounds:

    | Arm B result | Point estimate | True acceptance is at least | vs the ≥ 95 % gate |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | **120/120** | 100.00 % | **97.53 %** | **clears** |
    | **119/120** | 99.17 % | **96.11 %** | **clears** |
    | 118/120 | 98.33 % | 94.85 % | does not clear |
    | 117/120 | 97.50 % | 93.67 % | does not clear |

    Between the two arms, the resolvable difference is **≈ 2.5 percentage points**. **So this run can rule out a quality cost large enough to breach the gate, and it cannot distinguish 100 % from 99 %.** That is the honest limit and it is stated in advance: a 1-point true difference will read as noise here and **must not** be reported as evidence of no difference — which is precisely the error item 28(d) records.

    **(c) The decision rule, fixed now.**

    - **≥ 119/120 accepted**, with `reject.schema` and `reject.shape` both at 0.00 % → the true rate clears the gate with margin. **The prose-schema removal is safe to make on this evidence, and C3's cost saving is available.**
    - **≤ 118/120** → the removal is **not** made. The lower bound has fallen through the gate, and a 12 % saving does not buy a gate breach.
    - **Any rejection reading `schema` or `shape`** → the removal is not made **regardless of the count**, because that is the prose copy doing structural work the projection was assumed to cover, and one such rejection is a mechanism rather than a rate.

    **(d) What this run is not.** It is not a measurement of order *quality* beyond acceptance — a well-formed order that is tactically worse would pass Stage A and count as accepted. Acceptance is what the gate is written in and what the arms can compare; **a semantic quality difference would be invisible here, and this item says so now rather than after the number arrives.**

31. **C3's quality half: both arms accepted 120/120, the pre-registered rule fired, and the prose schema is removed from the shipped prefix.** *(v1.8.14 — 240 orders on `claude-haiku-4-5`, 120 per arm, under the fifth grant. The decision rule was fixed in item 30 and pushed **before** this run; nothing below chose a threshold after seeing a number.)*

    **(a) The result.**

    | | Arm A — as shipped | Arm B — prose schema removed |
    |---|---|---|
    | Prefix | 17,756 B | **8,750 B** (−9,006, −50.7 %) |
    | Accepted | **120/120 (100.0 %)** | **120/120 (100.0 %)** |
    | `reject.schema` / `reject.shape` | 0.00 % / 0.00 % | **0.00 % / 0.00 %** |
    | Cache hits | 119/120 | 119/120 |
    | Cache read **per hit** — the figure the 4,096 minimum applies to | 7,608 tok *(constant on all 119)* | **5,118 tok** *(constant on all 119)* |
    | Cache read **averaged over all 120 rows** — the figure the cost row is computed from | 7,544.6 tok | 5,075.4 tok |
    | $/order · $/four-ship-hour | $0.001464 · $1.05 | **$0.001220 · $0.88** |

    *(v1.8.16 — the two cache rows were **one row reading "119/120 @ 5,075.4 tok"**, which reads as a per-hit value and is not one. It is the per-hit constant averaged over 120 rows including the uncached first request: `5,118 × 119/120 = 5,075.4`. The mean is correct for the cost column and wrong wherever the cache minimum is in view, because **the minimum applies to a single request**. Split rather than replaced, because both numbers are used and each is right for exactly one thing. §Corrections item 33(c).)*

    **(b) The rule fires, and it fires on the branch that was written down first.** Item 30 fixed it: *≥ 119/120 with `reject.schema` and `reject.shape` both 0.00 % → the removal is safe to make.* Arm B returned **120/120**, which bounds its true acceptance at **≥ 97.53 %** (exact, one-sided 95 %) against the **≥ 95 %** gate. **The removal is made** — in `PromptRenderer::build`, and it is the first shipped-code change any Phase 3 diagnostic has produced.

    **(c) What this does not license, restated because item 30 said it in advance.** The arms **cannot** distinguish 100 % from 99 %; the resolvable difference is ~2.5 points. And **acceptance is not quality** — an order that is well-formed but tactically worse passes Stage A and counts here as accepted. **What is established is that removing the prose copy does not push the acceptance rate through the gate.** It is not established that the two prompts produce equally good orders, and no sentence in this document should be read as saying so.

    **(d) The saving is bigger than v1.8.5's, for a reason worth keeping.** 12 % there against **16.6 %** here, because that arm cut 6,780 bytes of *doctrine* and this one cuts **9,006 bytes of duplicated schema**. §Corrections item 22 predicted the post-removal cached block at ~5,345 tokens; measured **5,075**, **−5 %**. **That is the first prediction in this document's cost history to land inside 10 %**, and it landed because it was computed from a measured `usage` figure rather than scaled from a ratio.

    **(e) And the new constraint the change creates, which is the part a later editor will trip over.** *(Corrected v1.8.16 on two counts — §Corrections item 33(b) and 33(c). This subsection originally compared arm A's **per-hit** 7,608 against arm B's **120-row mean** 5,075, which are two different conventions inside one sentence, and priced the cliff at **5.7×**, which is unsourced and understates it by ≈3.4×. Both numbers below are now per-hit, and the multiplier is shown as arithmetic rather than asserted.)*

    The cached block falls from **7,608 to 5,118 tokens per request** against Haiku 4.5's **4,096** minimum. **The margin was 3,512 tokens (86 %); it is now 1,022 (24.9 %).** §Corrections item 22 concluded that item 21's cache-cliff warning was overstated — *"a page of doctrine can be deleted without consequence"*. **That is no longer true.** It holds up to roughly **1,020 tokens** — about 4,040 bytes of prefix at this corpus's measured 3.955 B/token — and fails after that.

    **What failing costs**, computed from the post-change state rather than quoted as a ratio of two pre-change rows:

    ```
    the saving this removal bought      $1.05 - $0.88                    = $0.17 / four-ship-hour
    the cost of losing the cache        (179.7 + 5,118) tok x $1/MTok
                                        + 106.2 tok x $5/MTok            = $0.005829 / order
                                        x 720 orders                     = $4.20 / four-ship-hour
                                        - $0.88 currently paid           = $3.32 / four-ship-hour
    ```

    **≈19× the saving, or ≈4.8× the current cached cost** — against the **5.7×** this subsection printed until v1.8.16, which was `$5.98 ÷ $1.05`, the uncached-versus-cached ratio of the **pre-change** prefix, attached to a saving it is not a multiple of. **The cliff warning was overstated when it was written and it is now approximately correct**, which is what happens when the thing a margin protects gets spent — and the number describing it was wrong in the direction that made spending the margin look cheaper than it is.

    **(f) One byte, and why it is in this item.** The first cut of the code change also deleted the blank line that had separated the schema block from `DOCTRINE:`, making the shipped prefix **8,749** bytes against the **8,750** that arm B measured. A one-byte divergence between the artifact under test and the artifact in production — invisible, harmless, and exactly the shape of every other item in this section. **The newline was restored and the reason written into the source**, so the prefix that ships is byte-identical to the prefix that was measured.

    **(g) Cost.** 240 orders ≈ **$0.32** against ≈$0.40 estimated. Running total ≈ **$2.48 of $5**.

    **C3 CLOSES.** Both halves are now measured: the cost half in v1.8.5 and again here, the quality half here. The change it proposed is made.

32. **C1: the hosted backend ran inside the engine, against real scenario state, and it works — and the harness printed two numbers that must not be quoted.** *(v1.8.15 — `run-live-scenario.ps1 -Backend claude`, 600 s commander-on plus a 600 s commander-off control, on `claude-haiku-4-5` against `oppint_red_interceptor` in the shipped "Mariana Shield". Under the fifth grant (v1.8.11). **19 checks, 0 failed.**)*

    **This is the run that was held across four grants.** Every hosted figure in this document before it described **six synthetic fixtures** — the same field set as a real snapshot, populated with values invented for a test. This one draws them from a shipped scenario. **The distinction was never technical; it was whose decision it was.**

    **(a) It works, and the parts worth naming are the ones a fixture cannot exercise.**

    | | |
    |---|---|
    | Plugin load, namespace, AIC-ARCH-4 probe | pass |
    | Backend actually hosted | `backend=claude enabled=true` **asserted**, not assumed |
    | Entities commanded | **both** — RedSu35_01 and RedSu35_02 |
    | Postures observed | **3 distinct** — `defend`, `engage`, `ingress` |
    | `reject.schema` / `reject.shape` | **0 % / 0 %** |
    | Timeouts | **0**, including the first order of the run |
    | Plugin frame cost | p50 **0.0023 ms**, max **2.87 ms** over 12,001 frames — inside the 5 ms bound |
    | Stage-B fratricide rejections | 0 |
    | Release tree afterwards | **clean** — config removed, `oppint_red_interceptor.lua` restored to 19,032 bytes |

    **(b) C3's change is confirmed on the product, not just on fixtures — and the agreement is EXACT.** *(Corrected v1.8.16 — §Corrections item 33(c). This subsection read "…one commit after it was measured on fixtures at 5,075", presenting a 43-token discrepancy between the engine and the fixtures. **There is no discrepancy. The fixtures measured 5,118 too.** 5,075.4 is that same constant averaged over 120 rows including the uncached first request — an artifact of this document's own averaging, reported as a measurement. The correction makes the claim stronger, which is why it is worth making.)*

    A real in-engine request reported `cache_read_input_tokens: **5,118**`. C3's arm B measured **5,118 on every one of its 119 cache hits**. The reduced prefix, caching in the engine, on real scenario state, one commit after it was measured on fixtures — **at the identical figure, not a close one**. **The shipped artifact behaves as the arm that authorized it did**, and there is no residual to explain.

    **(c) The most valuable single observation is a rejection.** One order was rejected `clamp`: the model asked for `cruiseSpeedMps` **450** against `safety.maxSpeedMps` **400**, and Stage B refused it. **That is Goal 3 — "no invalid, hallucinated, or unsafe order ever reaches a `request*` verb" — demonstrated on the product rather than on a corpus.** The rejection carried its full `rawBody`, which is AIC-DET-1 doing what v1.7.5 added it for. **A clean run would have been weaker evidence than this one.**

    **(d) And now the two numbers the harness printed that are not what they look like.**

    **The acceptance rate had the wrong denominator.** It printed **"10 of 13 requested (76.9 %)"**. Thirteen were requested, ten accepted, one rejected — **two were still in flight when the engine stopped**, having been issued in the last seconds of a fixed-length run. They have no verdict because the run did not wait for one, and counting them against acceptance charges the backend for a decision it was never allowed to make. Resolved: **10 of 11 (90.9 %)**. **Neither figure is a rate at n=11**, and this document has said so twice already — C5 records that "11 waypoint orders cannot establish a rate." **76.9 % reads exactly like an order-quality result and is not one, which is the same shape as the 91.7 % configuration artifact in item 24(b).** The script now reports resolved orders and names the in-flight count.

    **The "p95" was the maximum.** It printed **"p95 order latency: 5552 ms"** over **ten** samples, where the 95th-percentile index lands on the last one. The ten were **2,816 / 2,826 / 2,927 / 2,963 / 3,061 / 3,137 / 3,194 / 3,217 / 3,665 / 5,552 ms** — a median of **3,137 ms** and one outlier that became the headline. **PRD v1.7.4's Finding 3 recorded precisely this — "the reported p95 is not a p95", 10,363 ms being the second-highest of five — and this script went on printing one for four revisions after that finding was written.** A recorded lesson that stayed in the changelog and never reached the instrument. The script now reports min/median/max with n, and refuses to print a percentile.

    **(e) What C1 establishes, stated narrowly.** The hosted path works end to end inside the engine on real scenario state: real component reads, Stage B against real entity state, the Lua tier consuming published orders, the safety bound holding, the cache reading, the frame budget intact. **What it does not supply is any rate or percentile** — ~13 orders in ten minutes cannot, and the ≥ 95 % and latency bars stay where they are, on the soak. **The honest sentence this run buys is: "the backend works," in place of "the backend works on fixtures."** That is all it was ever for, and it is not a small thing.

    **(f) Cost.** 13 orders ≈ **$0.02** against ≈$0.10 estimated. Running total ≈ **$2.50 of $5**.

    **C1 CLOSES.**

33. **What a post-merge review of PRs #12 and #13 found: a guard this document says exists and does not, a cliff warning wrong by 3.4× in the flattering direction, and a per-hit figure reported as a mean three times over.** *(v1.8.16 — review written 2026-08-05 against `ddb459e`, recorded at `docs/review-2026-08-05-merged-prs-12-13.md`. **No new request, no network, no cost.** Both PRs were merged without review; every finding here is fix-forward.)*

    **Why this is one item and not six.** The defects cluster, and the cluster is the finding: **they are all in the guard rails around the C3 change rather than in the change itself.** The shipped behaviour change is the best-evidenced thing in this document — pre-registered, paired, decision rule pushed before the run, byte-identity discipline written into the source. What failed is everything built to watch it: the cache-minimum guard, the warning that stood in for the guard, and the probe's headline assertion. **A measurement can be careful and its instruments careless at the same time, and this document had not been looking at the second half.**

    **(a) `UAC-AIC-BE-3`'s cache-minimum comparison did not exist, and this document asserted it in three places.** The UAC (`docs/prd.md:2025`) says startup logged `prefixBytes` *"and the derived token count against the configured model's cache minimum"*; AIC-BE-3 v1.8.2 calls it *"the only detector of a silent regression"*; §Cost model says *"AIC-BE-3's startup comparison stays as the guard."* **The startup line logs `prefixBytes=` and stops.** There is no token estimate, no `4096` constant, no comparison, no warning anywhere in `src/`, and no test asserting one. The claim entered in v1.3 as an acceptance criterion, was reasoned about in v1.8.2 and v1.8.4 as though it were running code, and was never written.

    **It matters most exactly now.** C3 spent 72 % of the margin the guard was meant to protect. The failure it does not catch: an editor trims ~1,000 tokens of doctrine — which §Corrections item 22 still told them was safe — the cached block drops under 4,096, prefix caching stops, and the per-order cost goes from **$0.001220 to ≈$0.005829**. Nothing fails, nothing warns, no test goes red. The only observable is `cache_read_input_tokens` falling to zero in an order log nobody diffs. **That is the "wrong silently" side of the distinction AIC-BE-3 v1.8.4 draws, in the one place this document argues it matters.**

    **The build-time half is now implemented and is the reason this item can be written without a run.** `tests/PromptRendererTests.cpp` pins the shipped prefix to **8,750 bytes** — read from the repository's own `data/doctrine.txt`, so a doctrine edit fails it — and pins the **1,818 bytes** `PromptRenderer::build` contributes around the doctrine, so a renderer edit fails it separately and with a different message. Both failure messages carry the arithmetic rather than the byte count, because **the number that matters is not the number that changed**: what caches is 5,118 tokens against a 4,096 minimum, and the prefix text is only ~2,212 of them. **Verified by breaking it on purpose** — deleting the deliberate bare `'\n'` at `src/PromptRenderer.cpp:95`, the exact one-byte edit item 31(f) records catching by hand, takes the suite to 116/118 with both new cases red.

    **The runtime half is NOT implemented, and this subsection is where that is recorded rather than left implied.** It cannot compare `prefix()`: v1.8.4 already established that reading the prefix alone is wrong by 69 % about the quantity it guards, and after C3 a naive `prefix()`-based check is wrong in the *other* direction — the prefix text is ~2,212 tokens and would emit a false shortfall warning on **every** run. It has to compare `cache_read_input_tokens`, and **that value does not reach the code that would compare it** — see (f). Carried as **C9**. **UAC-AIC-BE-3 is amended to describe what exists**, which is the correction: a UAC that asserts behaviour nobody wrote is a worse defect than a missing guard, because it is the thing that stops anyone writing it.

    **(b) The `5.7×` cliff warning is unsourced, does not reproduce, and understates the hazard by ≈3.4×.** Item 31(e) and the v1.8.14 changelog both read *"falling out of cache costs 5.7× what the prose removal just saved."* The multiplier reconstructs only as **`$5.98 ÷ $1.05`** — the uncached-versus-cached four-ship-hour **ratio** from §Cost model's table, computed on the **pre-change 7,608-token prefix**. That is a ratio of two costs. The sentence attaches it to a **saving**. The arithmetic, shown inline this time:

    ```
    saving from the removal      $1.05 - $0.88                          = $0.17 / four-ship-hour

    cost of falling out of cache, from the POST-change state:
      input  (179.7 + 5,118) tok x $1/MTok                              = $0.005298 / order
      output (106.2 tok)          x $5/MTok                             = $0.000531 / order
                                                                          ---------
                                                                          $0.005829 / order
      x 720 orders/four-ship-hour                                       = $4.20 / four-ship-hour
      - $0.88 currently paid                                            = $3.32 / four-ship-hour

    $3.32 / $0.17  =  19.5x the saving        $4.20 / $0.88  =  4.8x the current cached cost
    ```

    **Every reading reconstructible from this document's own figures lands between 15× and 19×. None lands on 5.7.** And the error is in the direction that **makes the cliff look survivable**, in the one paragraph that exists to warn about it: a reader weighing "5.7×" against a "24 % margin" judges the downside modest and trims doctrine. **A number that flatters the decision it informs is the specific failure this section exists to catch**, and it took an outside reader to catch this one.

    **(c) Cached-token figures are 120-row means presented as per-hit values, and one of them fabricates a discrepancy that does not exist.** The archived CSVs carry a **constant** `cacheReadTokens` on every hit: **7,608** on arm A and **5,118** on arm B, 119 rows each. The `7,544.6` and `5,075.4` this document reports are those constants averaged over all **120** rows, including the first, uncached request:

    ```
    7,608 x 119/120 = 7,544.6                5,118 x 119/120 = 5,075.4
    ```

    That average is the **right** number for §Cost model's rows — it is a per-order mean and the bill is per order. It is the **wrong** number everywhere the cache minimum is in view, because **the minimum applies to a single request**. Two consequences:

    - **Item 31(e) mixed conventions inside one sentence** — the per-hit 7,608 for "before", the 120-row mean 5,075 for "after". The real margin is `5,118 − 4,096` = **1,022 tokens (24.9 %)**, not 979 (23.9 %). Corrected in place.
    - **Item 32(b) is the one that actually misleads, and correcting it makes the result stronger.** It reads: *"a real in-engine request reported `cache_read_input_tokens: 5,118` … one commit after it was measured on fixtures at 5,075."* **The fixtures measured 5,118 too.** The engine and the fixtures agree **exactly**; the 43-token gap is an artifact of this document's own averaging, presented as a measurement. The claim *"the shipped artifact behaves as the arm that authorized it did"* was **true in a stronger form than the sentence supporting it**, and was resting on a mis-derived number. It now reads as an exact agreement, which is what it always was.

    **This is the same class as item 29(c) and item 28(a): reading one statistic as though it were another.** A per-order mean and a per-request value differ by a factor of 119/120 — 0.8 % — which is exactly why it survived three revisions. **An error small enough to look like rounding is the hardest kind to see and the easiest kind to repeat.**

    **(d) Item 29(f) closes a Haiku target with a Sonnet measurement, and this document's own findings say those are not interchangeable.** §Success metrics' latency row is model-specific: *"Claude Haiku 4.5: p95 ≤ 2.5 s"*. The headers-time figures that close C2 — mean 3,157 ms, p95 6,917 ms — come from `c2-ttft-armA-full-doctrine.csv` and `c2-ttft-armB-short-doctrine.csv`, **both `claude-sonnet-5`**. **Haiku's fixed term has never been measured.** The claim was nonetheless generalised without a hedge: *"it was never achievable on this path"*, *"the target is unreachable by any prompt-side change and always was."*

    **Item 24 established that tokenization is model-specific and item 28 is a sustained argument about not reading one model's data as another's** — and the totals differ materially, Sonnet's mean round trip 7,393 ms against Haiku's measured p95 of 4,615 ms. If Haiku's fixed term were ≈1,800 ms the latency row would still read **MISSED**, but the *cause* C2 closes on would be wrong and "unreachable by any prompt-side change" would be unsupported. **The verdict survives; the scope of the reason does not.** Both sentences are rescoped to `claude-sonnet-5`, and the Haiku headers-time measurement is filed as **C10** — the archived request bodies plus `measure-ttft.ps1` would answer it for ≈$0.10 whenever a grant next exists. **It is not proposed, requested, or made here**, and §Success metrics still reads MISSED either way.

    **(e) Item 31 cites two different arm-A figures nine lines apart** — `7,544.6` in the table at (a), `7,608` in the prose at (e) — with no distinction drawn. Both are defensible; they are the 120-row mean and the per-hit constant of the same run. Appearing in one item as though interchangeable is (c) again, at close range. Both are now labelled where they appear.

    **(f) And a `SHALL` that is not met, found while establishing why (a)'s runtime half is not free.** AIC-BE-2 requires that *"`usage.cache_read_input_tokens` SHALL be recorded alongside"* the token counts, on the reasoning that *"without it there is no way to distinguish a cache hit from a miss."* `ClaudeLlmClient` parses the field into a member and **it stops there**: `LlmResult` carries `tokensIn` and `tokensOut` and **no cache field at all**, so the value never crosses into `CandidateOrder`, never reaches `OrderRecorder`, and **never appears in an order log**. It is readable only through the concrete adapter pointer, which is why `tests/live/LiveMain.cpp` holds one.

    **Every cached-token figure in this document came from the live harness, never from the product's own record.** That is not wrong — the harness reads the same field from the same response — but it means the detector AIC-BE-2 specifies for exactly the failure (a) is about does not exist on the product path either. **The same missing field blocks both halves**, which is why they are carried together as **C9** rather than as two items. No code change is made here: it is an FR-behaviour change and it does not belong on a review-fix branch.

    **(g) The instrument defects, recorded as a group because they are one habit.** `tests/live/measure-ttft.ps1`'s headline guard — the one item 29(a) cites as *"asserts the byte delta rather than trusting it"*, offered as the countermeasure to item 22 — **could not fail**: both sides of the comparison were the same arithmetic over the same literal. Its JSON parse ran on the original body and never on the spliced one that goes on the wire, so nothing checked that what it transmits is well-formed at all. Its `Expect100Continue` fix is a silent no-op under PowerShell 7, which would reintroduce the ~30,500 ms artifact item 29(g) paid to discover. Its `Pct()` printed a p95 with no minimum-n guard — **the same defect item 32(d) removed from `run-live-scenario.ps1` in the same revision, left standing in its sibling**. And `--no-prose-schema` could no longer succeed at all once C3 landed, so **arm A had become unreconstructible from the binary**.

    All are fixed, none needed a run, and the reconstruction was verified offline: `--mode prefix --prose-schema` writes **17,756 bytes**, arm A byte-exactly. **The pattern worth keeping is the first one.** Item 29(a) offered that assertion as evidence of care, and this document quoted it as such. **A guard with a confident comment and no teeth is worse than no guard**, because the comment is what stops the next reader from looking — and it was written in the revision whose subject was a probe measuring the wrong object.

34. **A phase that ran for eleven revisions and never had a section, a gate, or a close; a budget line stale by $2.10; and two of three key hypotheses with no verdict.** *(v1.8.17 — found while answering the question "what remains from the PRD, and what should we fix now?", which turned out to be unanswerable from this document without reading five egress grants and six §Corrections items. **No new request, no network, no cost.**)*

    **Why this is one item.** Nothing here is a defect in the product, in a measurement, or in a number derived from one. **They are the same failure at three scales: this document is careful about the things it measures and careless about the frame those measurements sit in.** Item 33 found the guard rails around a good measurement to be defective. This one finds the **container** missing — the phase that closed four carried items and produced the project's only shipped-code diagnostic was never written down; the section that spends the budget stopped tracking it after the first grant; and the section that owns hypotheses has been silent on two of them, one with conclusive data and one with none. **None of it is discoverable by measuring harder**, which is presumably why eleven revisions of increasingly careful measurement went straight past it.

    **(a) Phase 3 ran from v1.8.5 to v1.8.16 with no §Rollout section.** *"Phase 3"* appears in this document as a **destination** in twelve places. Four carried rows say they CLOSED *in* it. Three egress grants — the third, fourth, and fifth — were asked for, given, and spent against it, ≈**$2.10** in total. And §Rollout ended at Phase 2. **No deliverables list, no validation gate, no closing statement** — the three things Phase 0, 1a, 1b, and 2 each carry, and the three things that make "is this phase done?" a question with an artifact behind it rather than an archaeology exercise.

    The consequence is not cosmetic and it is measurable in this document's own terms: **there was nothing that could answer whether Phase 3 was over.** Both Phase 1b and Phase 2 close with an explicit banner and a carried list precisely so a later reader does not have to reconstruct the answer; Phase 3 had neither, and the reconstruction took five grants and six items to assemble. That is the same failure mode as OQ-4 sitting Open past its decision target for three revisions — **a state that nothing in the document was responsible for asserting**, which is what `lint-prd.ps1` exists for and what it does not check.

    **Written now, and labelled as reconstructed**, because a gate assembled after its own results is a different artifact from one written before them, and items 30 and 33 are both sustained arguments about that difference. **What keeps it from being retro-fitted is that not one row of the gate was chosen after seeing whether it passed:** every row is a carried item written down in v1.8.4, before any of it ran, with a dated close. The reconstruction assembles; it does not select.

    **(b) §Cost model's inputs table said `$0.40 spent` while ≈$2.10 more had been spent through it.** The row was **correct when written** — v1.8.2, before the third grant — and was never touched again across three grants and fourteen revisions. Meanwhile the running total was maintained **faithfully, somewhere else**: items 29(g), 31(g), and 32(f) each record it to the cent, and the fifth grant quotes *"$1.32 of $5"* in its own text. **The figure was tracked; the place a reader is told to look for it was not.**

    That is §Corrections item 21's shape exactly — *"a fact was corrected in one section and left standing in the section whose entire output is arithmetic over it"* — **recurring inside the very section item 21 was about.** And it propagated one step further, which is how a stale input becomes a wrong conclusion: §Cost model's recommendation still read *"the $5 balance funds roughly 4.7 hours"*, computed at the superseded **$1.05**/hour against a balance that is now **≈$2.50**. The real figure is **≈2.8 hours** — 40 % lower, from two independent stalenesses that pull in opposite directions and do not cancel. Both corrected, and the **per-grant ledger now lives in §Phase 3**, so the row has a source to be checked against rather than a number to be trusted.

    **(c) H1 and H3 carried no verdict in the section that exists to carry verdicts.** §Key hypotheses has annotated H2 since v1.7.4 — *MEASURED, NOT SUPPORTED*, with its arithmetic — and has said nothing about the other two. **They were missing for opposite reasons, and only one of them is fixable in a document revision.**

    - **H3's data is conclusive and was simply never written down.** `reject.schema` is **0.00 %** on every run that reports it, against a **< 1 %** bar, across **776 orders on two backends and three models** (200 local, 240 in the Phase 2 soak, 240 across C3's arms, 96 on Sonnet). §Success metrics has reported that row MET since v1.8.4. The verdict is written now, and **writing it exposed a second thing worth more than the annotation**: H3's stated validation is *"the same soak run twice"*, constrained against unconstrained, and **the unconstrained arm was never run.** So the honest verdict is *the constrained rate is far below the bar* — not *constrained decoding is why*, which is what the hypothesis actually asserts and what nobody measured. The closest evidence, §Corrections item 13, is on the **adjacent** counter (`reject.shape`, 10/12 → 0/12 on the schema encoding, unmoved by prompt wording). Recorded with that distinction intact rather than netted into a clean ✅.
    - **H1's data exists twice over and its instrument is a person.** Paired commander-on / commander-off runs were collected on the local backend in v1.7.4 and again on the hosted backend as part of C1 in v1.8.15. H1's signal is *"count of posture transitions per engagement that a **domain reviewer** marks appropriate given the situation"* — **no run produces that**, and this document said so correctly when it logged the runs: *"The review itself is a judgement and is not claimed here."* It was said once, in a gate table, and owned by nobody for thirteen revisions. It is now a named carried item with a destination, **C11**. **No verdict is written and none is implied**, because the failure being corrected here is precisely that a blank had started to read like one.

    **What none of this changes.** No measurement, no figure derived from a measurement, no gate result, and no §Success metrics row. **The latency row still reads MISSED, the cost row still reads MET at $0.88 per four-ship-hour, and the running total is unchanged at ≈$2.50 of $5.** This item moves no number. It puts numbers that already existed in the places the document was already telling readers to look.

35. **The cache-accounting seam: one missing field blocked an unmet `SHALL`, an unwritten guard, and a cost figure nobody could see — and the third turns out to be what makes the second possible.** *(v1.8.18 — specification only. **No new request, no network, no cost.** Written **before** the code, which is the ordering §Scope authority requires and the inverse of what item 33 had to do as a review-fix.)*

    **Why this is one item and not three.** C9 and C4 were opened fourteen revisions apart, for different reasons, and read as unrelated: one is a guard, one is a cost field. They are the same seam, and the reason they must land together is not tidiness. **It is that the guard cannot be written correctly without C4's field.** That is established below rather than asserted, and it is the one genuinely new fact in this revision — everything else here is specification of things this document has already argued for.

    **(a) The state of the seam, read out of the tree.** `ClaudeLlmClient` parses `usage.cache_read_input_tokens` into a private member and stops (`src/ClaudeLlmClient.cpp`). `LlmResult` carries `tokensIn` and `tokensOut` and no cache field, so the value never crosses `runWorkerCall`'s boundary into `CandidateOrder`, never reaches `OrderRecorder`, and **has never appeared in an order log**. `usage.cache_creation_input_tokens` is parsed by nothing at all. The only reader is `tests/live/LiveMain.cpp`, through a concrete `ClaudeLlmClient*` it holds for exactly that purpose — which is why **every cached-token figure in this document came from the harness and none from the product**.

    **(b) The discriminator, and why C4 stops being optional.** A prompt block below the configured model's cache minimum **does not cache, and says nothing**: no error, no rejection, no counter. What it returns is `cache_creation_input_tokens: 0`. A **cold but eligible** first request — the normal opening of every run — returns a **non-zero** `cache_creation_input_tokens` (it wrote the block) with `cache_read_input_tokens` at zero (there was nothing yet to read). The two states are therefore separable on the pair and **not** on the read field alone:

    | `cache_creation_input_tokens` | `cache_read_input_tokens` | What happened | Guard |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | `> 0` | `0` | **Cold start.** The block was eligible and was written. Expected exactly once per run | silent |
    | `0` | `≥ the model's minimum` | Steady-state hit. The 119-of-120 case in C3's arms | silent |
    | `0` | `0` | **The block never cached at all.** The failure this guard exists for | **warn** |

    **This is the whole argument for landing C4 with C9.** A guard reading only `cache_read_input_tokens` sees `0` for both the first row and the third, so it either **fires on the first request of every run** — and is muted by the first operator who meets it, which makes it worse than absent, because a muted guard still reads as a guard in this document — or it suppresses the first response of a run and thereby **cannot detect a shortfall that begins at the first response**, which is the only way this failure ever begins. **C4's row in §Carried out of Phase 2 said "add alongside `lastCacheReadTokens()` when a cheaper reason to touch that interface arises." The cheaper reason never arrives; the field is a precondition, and the row was wrong about its own priority.**

    **(c) The guard's shape, corrected on two counts.** It is **not a startup comparison**, and `UAC-AIC-BE-3` has said so since v1.8.16 without the specification catching up: `cache_read_input_tokens` exists only *after* a response, so a check that runs at `initialize()` has nothing to read. And it **SHALL NOT** be written against `prefix()`. v1.8.4(a) established that reading the prefix alone is wrong by **69 %** about the quantity it guards, in the flattering direction; after C3 it is wrong in the *other* direction — the prefix text is **~2,212 tokens** against Haiku 4.5's **4,096** minimum, so a `prefix()`-based check would emit a **false shortfall on every single run**. The correct shape is a **per-response check on the simulation thread**, evaluated where the candidate is already being counted and recorded, on the two fields the response actually reports.

    **(d) The model → cache-minimum table, derived rather than carried.** These three numbers have appeared in AIC-BE-3's acceptance criterion since v1.3 and have never been re-checked against the vendor's published figures. They are re-derived here and they hold:

    | Model | Minimum cacheable prefix |
    |---|---|
    | `claude-haiku-4-5` — **the default** | **4,096 tokens** |
    | `claude-sonnet-5` | **1,024 tokens** |
    | `claude-opus-5` | **512 tokens** |

    **What matters more than the three values is a property of the series: it is not monotonic.** Neighbouring generations of the same tier differ — 2,048 and 4,096 both appear elsewhere in the same family — so **the minimum for a model not in this table SHALL NOT be interpolated, scaled, or assumed from its tier.** That is item 24's lesson (tokenization is model-specific) recurring on a different axis, and it is why the guard treats an unrecognised `claude.model` as *unknown* rather than guessing a bound.

    **(e) The record gains both fields on rejections as well as acceptances.** C4 and C9 asked only that the values reach the order log; AIC-DET-1 is widened one step further, because the narrow reading preserves a hole this document already measured. `OrderRecorder::recordRejected` writes **no token field at all** — and §Corrections item 27(d) records the case that makes that expensive: four truncated Sonnet orders were **billed for 512 output tokens each and produced nothing**. A rejected order costs real money, and the record AIC-DET-1 calls the account of a run cannot currently show it. **A cost field that is only written when the order was good is not a cost field.**

    **(f) Where the evidence lives, which C11 needs and never specified.** §Carried out of Phase 2 C11 rests on paired commander-on / commander-off logs *"retained for the domain review"* and names **no location**. They were written to `%TEMP%\aic-live` and survived three days by luck. Worse, `tests/smoke/run-live-scenario.ps1` **deleted the order log at the start of every run**, so the 2026-08-03 run's log is gone. The convention is written into §Source control now: order logs and engine logs are **archived outside the repository** — `logs/` and `*.jsonl` are security-relevant ignore rules that `check-artifacts.ps1` enforces, so in-tree is not available and never was — and the harness **timestamps rather than deletes**. **The largest open item in this document was resting on files with no home.**

    **What this item does not do.** It makes no measurement and authorizes none. Every figure it cites — 5,118 cached tokens, the 1,022-token margin, $0.001220 against $0.005829 per order — is quoted from items 31 through 33 and is not re-derived here. **No grant is sought and none is needed**: the seam is testable end to end against a fake transport through the injectable factory the adapter suite already uses.

36. **C10 ran, and it takes half of C2's explanation away from the model that actually ships.** *(v1.8.20 — 48 orders on `claude-haiku-4-5`, six synthetic `LiveMain` fixtures × 8 repeats, under the sixth grant (v1.8.19). **≈$0.0645 against ≈$0.065 estimated.** Rows archived at `tests/live/data/c10-ttft-haiku-fixed-term.csv`.)*

    **The result, against the pre-registered pair.** Item 33(d) rescoped C2's conclusion to `claude-sonnet-5` and carried Haiku's fixed term as unmeasured. The sixth grant wrote both outcomes down in advance. **The second one landed.**

    | Fixed term (time to response headers) | `claude-sonnet-5` *(item 29)* | `claude-haiku-4-5` *(this run)* |
    |---|---|---|
    | mean | **3,157 ms** | **2,452 ms** |
    | p50 | — | **1,510 ms** |
    | p95 | **6,917 ms** | **3,811 ms** or **5,263 ms** — see (c) |
    | min / max | — | 835 ms / 27,471 ms |
    | over 2,500 ms on its own | — | **7 of 48 (14.6 %)** |

    **(a) C2's sentence does not survive intact on the default model.** C2 closed on: *"headers alone, before one token exists, are mean 3,157 ms / p95 6,917 ms, so the fixed term exceeds the 2.5 s total-latency target and no prompt-side change can reach it."* On Haiku the **median** request's fixed term is **1,510 ms**, which leaves roughly **a second of headroom under the target**, and **85.4 % of requests** clear 2,500 ms on the fixed term alone. **The claim that the floor alone rules the target out is a Sonnet property.** Item 33(d) suspected the generalisation was unsafe; it was, and this is the measurement that says so rather than the argument that suspected it.

    **(b) What does survive, and it is the half that matters for the gate.** §Success metrics states the target at **p95**, and at p95 the fixed term still exceeds 2,500 ms on Haiku under either convention below. **The latency row still reads MISSED — total p95 is 7,238 ms — exactly as the grant pre-registered.** So the verdict is untouched and the *reason* is now two reasons: on Sonnet the floor rules the target out outright; **on Haiku the floor does not, and the miss is driven by variance instead.**

    **(c) The p95 is reported twice on purpose, because at n = 48 it is not a single number.** Nearest-rank gives **5,263 ms**; the floor convention gives **3,811 ms**. The gap is entirely two outliers — 10,482 ms and 27,471 ms — and the p95 index straddles them. **This document has recorded the same hazard twice** (v1.7.4 Finding 3; item 32(d), where a "p95" over ten samples was the maximum wearing a percentile's name), so it is not going to quietly pick the convention that flatters the sentence it is writing. **Both are stated; neither changes (a) or (b).**

    **(d) The variance is the finding, not the floor — and it is not the cold start.** SD is **3,977 ms** on a quantity that is supposed to be fixed. Excluding the two requests over 10 s, the fixed term is mean **1,734 ms**, p50 **1,491 ms**, max **5,263 ms**. **Both outliers are mid-run (orders 24 and 43) and both were fully cached at 5,118 tokens**, so neither is the cache write: the uncached first request came back in **3,738 ms**, unremarkable. Two ordinary, fully-cached requests took 10.5 s and 27.5 s to return **headers**. That is service-side queueing, and it is the one explanation left standing for Haiku's p95 miss — **not the prefix, not output length, and not a floor that prompt work could lower.**

    **What this does not license.** It is one arm at n = 48 on synthetic fixtures, and it supplies **no rate and no remedy**. It does not reopen C2 — C2's verdict was that the target is missed, and it still is. It does not propose a latency-target change, a model change, or a config change; the sixth grant authorized **measurement only** and no second arm follows. **And it does not explain the outliers**, which would need repeats rather than a larger single sample — the same distinction C8 records about ceilings sized against noise.

    **(e) The estimate held, which is worth recording because this project's estimates mostly have not.** ≈**$0.0645** actual against ≈**$0.065** derived — **+0.8 %**. The Phase 3 ledger's other rows ran +74 %, ±0 %, +68 % and −80 %. The difference is that this figure was **derived from measured per-order components** rather than scaled from a prior run — and the run's own `tokensIn` mean came back at **179.7** and `tokensOut` at **106.0**, matching §Cost model's assumed inputs almost exactly. **§Cost model's per-order arithmetic for Haiku is now confirmed against an independent run**, which is a better result for that section than anything in item 34 was able to give it.

    **C10 CLOSES.** Running total **≈$2.57 of $5**.

37. **The `engage` posture has never fired a weapon at an enemy aircraft, and the precondition that stopped it was prescribed by this document.** *(v1.8.21 — found while answering a reviewer's question during the H1 review: *"why can't I see the weapons fired by the red team Su-35s? Have they launched at all?"*. Three instrumented 150 s runs of "Mariana Shield" on the `local` backend, 2026-08-06. **No new request, no network, no cost.** The instrumentation was reverted; the fix is specified here before the code, per §Scope authority.)*

    **(a) What was measured.** The reference script's `considerFiring` returns silently at every guard and discards `requestFire`'s boolean, so the engine log could not say which guard stopped the shot. Naming each outcome and sampling `canFire` independently of posture produced this, with an `engage` order in force naming a reported target:

    | Run | Instrumentation | Result |
    |---|---|---|
    | 1 | fire-path outcomes only | No `engage` ordered in 150 s — the fire path was never reached. **The gate went unobserved, which is why it survived Phase 1b.** |
    | 2 | + posture-independent `canFire` probe | `engage (BlueF16_01)` lands, then **`canFire=false rounds=6 isValid=true`** — constant for the whole run, both aircraft |
    | 3 | + gate observed rather than enforced | **`requestFire(2-arg) → true`**, and `Weapon spawn request emitted: RedSu35_02_wpn_22600 … at target BlueF16_01` |

    **The verb works and the ammunition is present. The precondition is wrong.** Run 3 also rules out the second candidate: the two-argument *"legacy profile selection"* form of `requestFire` needs no explicit hardpoint to succeed.

    **(b) Why AIC-ORD-2 carries the defect and not just the script.** The `engage` row has prescribed `weapon.canFire(entityId)` since v1.0, so a conforming script was obliged to call it. §Tenet 5 says verb arities come from the generated stubs — and the stub says `canFire(entityId)`, **carrier only**, while describing *"armed, in range, ammo > 0"*. A range predicate with no target argument cannot be answering the question the `engage` row asked. **The evidence that it was the wrong verb was in the release tree the whole time:** `oppint_red_interceptor.lua` — the OQ-6 pick, chosen precisely because *"its Tier-1 logic is the quality bar"* — fires reliably and **never calls `canFire`**. Phase 1b compared the two scripts' behaviour and did not compare their fire paths.

    **(c) The gate was load-bearing for something else, which is the part a narrow fix would miss.** Ungated, the script fired **66 times in ~130 s** — one launch per tick. The stock script spaces shots with an assessment window (`nextFireTime = now + assessS`); the reference script has no equivalent, and never needed one because nothing ever got past `canFire`. **Deleting the gate alone would replace "never fires" with "empties the rail in three seconds".** AIC-ORD-2 therefore gains a re-engagement-interval obligation and a checked-return obligation alongside the removal, with acceptance criteria for both.

    **(d) A claim made during this investigation is corrected here rather than dropped.** The commanded aircraft were reported as taking **zero** launches against 2–4 for the control. That count came from a pattern that matched only target-bearing launch lines. **The corrected figures:**

    | Run | Commander-on | Commander-off (stock script) |
    |---|---|---|
    | 2026-08-05 hosted | 2 × `entity_MunitionTarget` | 3 × `BlueF16_01`, 1 × `BlueF16_02` |
    | 2026-08-06 11:04 local | 2 × `entity_MunitionTarget` | 2 × `BlueF16_01`, 1 × `BlueF16_02` |
    | 2026-08-06 11:10 local | 2 × `entity_MunitionTarget` | 1 × `BlueF16_01`, 1 × `BlueF16_02` |

    They do launch. **Not one commanded launch in any archived run is at a Blue aircraft** — every one is at `entity_MunitionTarget`, a placeholder, emitted before the first order lands — while every control launch is at a real fighter. **The count was wrong and the conclusion it was offered in support of is now established by mechanism instead of by counting**, which is the stronger footing and was available only because the wrong number was checked.

    **(e) What this does and does not do to H1.** The commanded entities in every H1 pair were, in effect, unarmed: they lost engagements they never shot in. **No outcome-based comparison** — survival, shots per kill, time-to-first-shot, the harder signals §Rabbit holes proposed as H1 alternatives — **can be drawn from the archived pairs**, and any that has been should be withdrawn. H1's *stated* signal is unaffected: it asks whether a domain reviewer marks the posture transitions appropriate, and an `engage` order can be the correct intent whether or not the tier below it executes. **The review recorded in §Key hypotheses stands; an outcome comparison built on these logs would not.**

    **(f) And one gate result is now known to have been vacuous.** C1's live smoke records **"Zero fratricide ✅ 0"**. Nothing the commanded aircraft did could have produced a fratricide, because nothing they fired was aimed at an aircraft. It is not a false entry — it is a true one carrying no information, and it should not be cited as evidence that the safety envelope prevented anything.

    **(g) The first uncounfounded pair was then run, and it moves the explanation from the plumbing to the model.** 600 s commander-on / commander-off on `local`, same seed, with the fix in place *(2026-08-06, `20260806T144058Z-local`)*:

    | | Commander-on *(fixed script)* | Commander-off *(stock Tier 1)* |
    |---|---|---|
    | Accepted orders | 5 — **4 × `hold`, 1 × `ingress`, zero `engage`** | — |
    | Red launches at a Blue aircraft | **0** | **4** |
    | Red detonations on a Blue aircraft | **0** | **2**, both on `BlueF16_01` |
    | Red losses | both by ~85 s | both by ~85 s |

    **The commanded aircraft did not fire because they were never ordered to engage** — not because they could not. The fix is verified separately: a 150 s run on the same build landed an `engage` and produced `RedSu35_02 launching at BlueF16_01 (22244 m, assess 30 s)`, one launch and one spawn, correctly spaced. **What this pair measures is posture selection**, and it agrees with the H1 marks from the same backend: the local model issued **no `engage` in 600 s** while its two `inappropriate` marks were both `hold` decisions where the reviewer judged action was required. **The commander's disadvantage in this pair is a model property, not a defect** — which is a claim item 37 could not have made before the gate was found, because until then every pair was confounded.

    **What it still does not license.** One run, one model, n=5 accepted orders. **It is not an H1 verdict** — H1's instrument is the reviewer, and a local-model outcome does not speak to whether posture-level intent at a 15–30 s cadence is sound. The hosted arm, which issued five `engage` orders across its run, has **not** been re-paired under the fix and would need a grant.

    **And the `reject.shape` tally moves again:** **1 of 10 (10 %)** this run, `posture 'hold' requires orbitRadiusM > 0` — the same conditional value rule as before. Post-C3 local now stands at **4 of 32 (12.5 %)** against a pre-C3 baseline of 0 of 200. Still carried, still undecided.

    **C12 opens** — see the register. Running total unchanged at **≈$2.57 of $5**.

38. **C12 closes on the arity this project chose, not on a broken seam — and the first clean live smoke in the project's history immediately exposes the next thing.** *(v1.8.22 — one 150 s `local` run, 2026-08-06. **No new request, no network, no cost.** H1's verdict is recorded in §Key hypotheses under the same revision and **C11 closes**.)*

    **(a) `requestFire`'s optional third argument is not optional in effect.** The stub calls `hardpointName` *"optional — omit for legacy profile selection"*, and item 37's fix omitted it. **The engine distinguishes the two forms in its own spawn line**, which is where this was visible all along:

    | Call | Engine spawn line | Draws a loadout slot |
    |---|---|---|
    | `requestFire(id, target)` | `… at target BlueF16_01 **profile** Weapon_AAM_MediumRange_ActiveRadar_Generic` | **No** |
    | `requestFire(id, target, hardpoint)` | `… at target BlueF16_01 **hardpoint** R77_BVR` | **Yes** |

    **That is the whole of C12.** Fired by profile, 66 launches left `ammoCount` at 6; **the seam was never broken** — the shipped SAM script uses the hardpoint form and reaches `RedSAM_Launcher winchester (SAM cell empty)` in the same runs. With the reference script switched to a named loaded hardpoint, the ammunition trace reads **`6 left` → `5 left`** across successive launches. **`winchester` is reachable for a commanded aircraft for the first time, and Stage-B check B8 — written in v1.7.3 — can now encounter the case it was written for.** C12 CLOSES.

    **(b) The live smoke passes 17 of 17 for the first time**, including the *"at least three distinct postures"* assertion that had failed in every prior run. **This is not claimed as an effect of the fix.** Posture variety is the model's output and the fix touches only the fire path; a single run that passes where others failed is one sample of a stochastic local model, and §Corrections has twice recorded what happens when a favourable single sample is read as a trend.

    **(c) What the working fire path made visible on its very first clean run: two of three commanded launches went at a munition.** `RedSu35_01` fired **twice** at `BlueF16_01_wpn_32300_6` — an inbound air-to-air missile — at 8.6 km and 12.6 km, spending two R-77s. The commander had issued `engage` naming that track. **Nothing rejected it, and each layer is behaving as specified:** Tier 1's reporting obligation forwards *every* sensor track, munitions included; Stage-B check B3 requires only that a named target **was reported**, which it was; and §Doctrine tells the model to `defend` against an inbound munition without ever saying a munition is not a valid `engage` target. **Three correct components compose into a wrong outcome**, which is the failure mode a two-stage validator is least able to catch — B3 is a provenance check, not a plausibility one.

    **This could not have been observed before this revision.** For the whole of Phases 1b through 3 no commanded aircraft ever fired, so an order naming an implausible target had no consequence and left no trace. **Item 37's defect was concealing an order-quality defect**, and the second was only reachable through the first. Carried as **C13** rather than fixed here, because the candidate remedies — a Stage-B check on target class, a doctrine line, or a filter on what Tier 1 reports — sit in three different layers and **choosing among them is a design decision, not a bug fix**; §Scope authority puts that in this document before any code.

39. **C13 closes in the layer that should hold it, and the capability floor H1 left unmeasured turns out to sit inside `local` rather than between `local` and hosted.** *(v1.8.23 — Stage-B check B9 specified before the code; one 600 s paired `local` run at `qwen2.5:14b-instruct-q4_K_M`, 2026-08-06. **No new request, no network, no cost.**)*

    **(a) B9, and why two other layers were rejected.** The fix could have gone in the doctrine, in Tier 1's reporting, or in Stage B. **A doctrine line was rejected on this project's own measurement:** H1's verdict records a 7B model ignoring §Doctrine's survival-first rule with a munition inbound at 18 km, so a check that works only when the model reads it is not a check. **Filtering Tier 1's reported tracks was rejected because it costs the posture it protects:** `defend` exists to answer inbound munitions and cannot choose them if they are removed from the picture, so suppressing them to prevent a bad `engage` would disable the correct response in order to block the incorrect one. **Stage B is the layer whose stated job is refusing well-formed, wrong orders**, it is model- and doctrine-independent, and it runs in the offline suite with no scenario loaded.

    **(b) The unknown-kind rule is the half worth arguing about.** B9 **passes** a target carrying no `entityType`. That is the opposite of B4, which **refuses** a target of unknown team, and the asymmetry is the point: an unknown team makes the shot more dangerous, while an unknown kind leaves it merely unlabelled — and refusing the latter would take every scenario whose profiles omit the field offline, converting a safety improvement into an outage. B4 still runs first, so an unknown-kind target on an unknown team is refused there regardless. **Asserted as its own test**, alongside a guard that a hostile *platform* is still engageable, because a check that rejects everything also passes a test that only looks for rejections.

    **(c) The capability floor, measured.** v1.8.22 closed H1 as *supported, model-dependent* and left the boundary between the failing 7B and the passing Haiku entirely unmeasured. One run at 14B narrows it:

    | | `qwen2.5:7b-instruct-q8_0` | `qwen2.5:14b-instruct-q4_K_M` |
    |---|---|---|
    | Distinct postures | `hold, ingress` — **assertion FAILED** | `crank, engage, hold` — **PASSED** |
    | `engage` orders in 600 s | **0** | **1**, plus a `crank` |
    | Launches at a Blue aircraft | **0** | **1** |
    | `reject.shape` | 1 of 10 (**10 %**) | 0 of 6 (**0 %**) |
    | Paired live smoke | 1 failed | **19/19 — the first clean pair this project has recorded** |

    **The useful form of this result is where the floor is, not that there is one.** *Local versus hosted* would have implied the feature needs egress to work at all. **7B versus 14B does not** — a 14B at Q4 is 9 GB against the verification host's 16 GB (OQ-2), so the shipped default backend can plausibly be made to work **without any network at all.** No default is changed here; C8 already records that a value picked from one run is picked against noise.

    **(d) It moves C14's question, and C14 opens anyway.** `reject.shape` was **0 of 6** at 14B against **1 of 10** at 7B. That is consistent with the mechanism this document proposed — a *conditional* value rule (`orbitRadiusM > 0` only when `posture == hold`) is what constrained decoding cannot enforce and what a smaller model is likeliest to miss — and **inconsistent with C3 having deleted prose the prompt needed**, which would have hurt both models. **n = 6 settles nothing**, and a favourable small sample is exactly the thing §Corrections has twice recorded this project mistaking for a result. **C14 is filed so the question is owned rather than closed by luck.**

    **(e) What this run does not license.** **3 accepted orders.** The 14B still **trails the stock control on outcome** — one launch and no hits against the control's two launches and one hit — so nothing here says the commander beats the script. **And the capability is bought with decision rate:** 6 requests in 600 s at 14B against the 7B's 10, on a cadence of 20 s, meaning the larger model misses windows the smaller one made. **That trade is unpriced** and is not the same question as C2's latency target. No rate and no percentile is claimed from either arm.

    **C13 CLOSES. C14 opens.** 134/134 unit tests, 5 new. Running total unchanged at **≈$2.57 of $5**.

    | Live smoke | **19/19** | **19/19** | **19/19** | **19/19** |
    | Distinct postures | 3 | 3 | 4 | 3 |
    | `engage` issued | yes | yes | **no** | **no** |
    | Commanded launches / hits | 1 / 0 | 1 / 0 | **0 / 0** | **0 / 0** |

    |---|---|---|---|
    | `qwen2.5:7b-instruct-q8_0`, 3 pairs | 18 / 27 | **66.7 %** | ≥ 90 % |

    - **C16 — `'reason' must be 1-200 characters, got 204`, twice, at exactly 204.** This is not the model failing; it is a **more verbose model meeting a cap this document chose**, and the whole order is discarded for a field that carries no control authority.
