41. **C15 is ours. The snapshot has never carried the aircraft's own speed, so the model reached for the nearest number that looked like one — and copied a signed velocity component.** *(v1.8.25 — offline diagnosis from the four archived 14B pairs and the shipped scenario seed, 2026-08-06. **No new request, no network, no cost.** C16's decision is recorded with it, because the two fixes ship together.)*

    **(a) The four rejections are one number, and the number names its own cause.** Item 40(c) recorded the reject *detail* and never read the value behind it. Recovered from `rawBody` in all four archived logs, the emitted value is **`-220.0` every time** — not a zero, and not four different wrong numbers. Every occurrence is `serial: 1`, the **first** order for that entity.

    | Run | Entity | t (s) | serial | emitted `cruiseSpeedMps` |
    |---|---|---|---|---|
    | 171041Z | `RedSu35_02` | 11.6 | 1 | **−220.0** |
    | 185024Z | `RedSu35_02` | 7.6 | 1 | **−220.0** |
    | 191037Z | `RedSu35_02` | 9.6 | 1 | **−220.0** |
    | 193051Z | `RedSu35_02` | 9.7 | 1 | **−220.0** |

    **(b) Where −220.0 comes from.** `data/resources/seed/realistic_scenario_seed_data.json` spawns both Su-35s at **`headingDeg: 270.0`, `speedMps: 220.0`**. Heading 270° is due west, so the NED velocity at spawn is **`velN 0, velE −220, velD 0`** — and `own.velN` / `own.velE` / `own.velD` are three of the own-ship fields §Exactly what is transmitted puts in the volatile suffix. **The model did not invent a speed. It copied `own.velE`.** The magnitude is exactly right and only the sign is wrong, because a signed component of a velocity vector is not a speed.

    **(c) Which makes this document's defect, on two counts, and the first is load-bearing.**

    - **The volatile suffix carries no scalar speed at all.** It hands the model three *signed components* and expects it to compute √(N²+E²+D²) to recover the one quantity the order asks for. Nothing in the prompt states that the components are signed, or that they are not speeds. **The nearest number to hand was wrong by exactly one sign**, which is a snapshot defect rather than a reasoning failure.
    - **The doctrine's CRUISE SPEED block gives nothing to anchor on.** It says *"Give a speed the posture can use"* and names no value, no band, and no floor, so a model with no own-speed field has only the situation block to reach into. **The block also states something false:** *"the aircraft will clamp anything outside its own envelope."* Nothing clamps. Stage A rejects against a static ceiling and Stage B's B6 rejects against `safety.maxSpeedMps` — the sentence describes a mechanism this system does not have, and it describes it in the reassuring direction.

    **(d) Why `RedSu35_02` and not `RedSu35_01`, which spawns identically.** Both aircraft start on the same heading at the same speed; what differs is *when* each is first asked. The number is available only to an aircraft still on its initial 270° leg when its first order is requested — which is why the failure is at `serial: 1` in all four runs and recurs at no later serial in any of them. **It is not a property of the entity; it is a property of the first snapshot.** Item 40's *"always on `RedSu35_02`"* gave the symptom's address rather than its cause, and the address is what made it look like a model quirk.

    **(e) The fix is a derived field, and the derivation matters more than the field.** §Exactly what is transmitted gains **`own.speedMps`**, computed as **‖velocityNed‖** over the three runtime columns already on the list. It is **derived from data already transmitted** — it reads nothing new from the engine and widens no trust boundary, so AIC-SEC-2's allowlist grows by a scalar that is a function of three rows already on it.

    **It is deliberately NOT read from `componentTransform/speedMps`, and that is the whole of the decision.** That schema leaf is documented in `schema-reference.json` as *"Initial ground speed at t=0"*, on a component whose own description says runtime motion is *"thereafter owned by the physics pass, not by this datablock."* Reading it would place a **spawn-time constant** in the snapshot and label it current — the same class of error as the one being fixed, in the same field, arriving by a route that looks more authoritative than the arithmetic. `TransformRuntimeColumns.h` declares **no runtime heading or speed column**; `velocityNed.*` is the only live motion state that exists, so a live speed **must** be derived and cannot be read.

    **(f) The same reading opens a question this item does not answer.** `own.headingDeg` is read from the schema leaf `componentTransform/headingDeg`, which the same authority documents as *"Initial heading: the compass direction the entity faces and travels in at **t=0**."* If that datablock is not written back by the physics pass — which is what its component description says — then **every prompt this project has sent has carried a spawn-time constant labelled as current heading.** That is **not asserted here.** It follows from the same document that produced (e), it has not been measured, and item 40 is a record of what concluding ahead of the measurement costs. Opened as **C18**.

**And the instrumentation it needs does not exist, which is the more useful half of this sub-item.** There is no prompt dump: `AIC-DET-1`'s `order.requested` record carries `promptHash` and `snapshotHash` and **no snapshot content**, so nothing an operator can run today shows what own-ship state was transmitted. `snapshotHash` cannot stand in for it — position moves every tick, so the hash changes whether or not heading does. Answering C18 therefore needs a **record-format change**, which is an FR-behaviour change and belongs in this document before it is in code. **It is deliberately not bundled into this revision**, because C15's fix removes the condition that made the snapshot's contents urgent and bundling an unrelated record change into a revision that already carries two closes is how a change arrives without its own argument. **C18 is open, cheap, and needs no grant** — and it is now open with its blocker named rather than with an instrument assumed available, which is the error §Corrections item 35(f) and the v1.8.18 checklist row are both about.

    **(g) C16 — the decision, and the cost basis the round number never had.** `reason` is advisory: AIC-ORD-1's field table has said *"never parsed"* since v1.0, and no verb, no posture, and no Stage-B check reads it. **A field that cannot change what the aircraft does cannot make an order unsafe by being long** — while rejecting on it discards the posture, the target, the waypoint and the ROE, every one of which does carry authority. AIC-VAL-2's ladder then holds the **previous** order in force, so an over-long rationale does not merely lose one order, it **extends a stale one**.

    **The cap therefore becomes a truncation rather than a rejection** — and the cap itself moves, because a cap sitting four characters under what a model naturally writes fires constantly and saves nothing.

    **What a cap on `reason` actually costs, stated rather than assumed.** `reason` is the only free-text field in the order document — every other field is an enum, a number, or an id — so it is the only part of the response whose length the model chooses. It is billed as **output tokens** ($5/MTok on Haiku 4.5) and written into `rawBody`, which `OrderRecorder` caps at **4,096 bytes** and truncates **silently, with no marker** (§Corrections item 26). At the corpus-measured **3.955 bytes/token**, 200 characters is ≈ **51 tokens** against a measured mean response of **106.2 tokens**: the cap was already governing roughly half a typical response, which is why a slightly more verbose model runs straight into it.

    **The new cap is 512 characters, derived from those two quantities rather than picked.** 512 characters is ≈ **129 tokens** — approximately **one measured-mean response** — which is the defensible line: past it, the advisory field costs more than the order it explains. Against the record cap it is comfortable rather than tight, at 512 characters plus the ~300 bytes the rest of the order document occupies, or **~20 % of the 4,096-byte record**, so **no legal `reason` can push a rejection record into silent truncation**. Worst-case marginal cost against the old cap is ~79 output tokens: **≈$0.0004/order, ≈$0.09 per four-ship-hour** at the 240-order rate, against a ≤ $1.10 target currently measuring $0.88. **Expected** cost is far below worst case — the observed overflow is 204 characters, so the model is not writing 512.

    **The lower bound stays a rejection, and the asymmetry is deliberate.** An empty `reason` is a signal that the model did not answer a required field; an over-long one is a signal about how verbose the configured model is. Only the second varies with which model is deployed, and only the second should therefore be absorbed rather than refused.

    **Truncation SHALL be marked.** §Corrections item 26 records `OrderRecorder`'s silent 4 KiB truncation as a defect precisely because a shortened record that does not say it was shortened is worse than a rejected one. A truncated `reason` therefore ends in a visible marker and increments a counter, so the order log shows what happened rather than merely showing a shorter sentence.

    **(h) Implementing (e) exposed a harness defect that would have invalidated the run meant to measure it.** Both the post-build deploy step and `run-live-scenario.ps1` copied `data/doctrine.txt` into the release tree **only when it was absent** — deliberately, so that an operator's tuned doctrine survives a rebuild. The consequence nobody had needed until now is that a doctrine **edit never reaches the engine**: the rewritten block is **7,824 bytes against the deployed 6,932**, the unit suite pins the new prefix, and a live run would have sent the old one. **The measurement and the artifact would have disagreed by 892 bytes with nothing red** — the same class of error as the **one-byte** prefix divergence item 31(f) records catching by hand, three orders of magnitude larger and sitting inside the run that was supposed to be the evidence. The smoke script now **backs up, overwrites, and restores** the doctrine on the same terms it already applied to the mission script and the deployed config, and asserts the deployed copy matches the repository's **by size** rather than merely existing. The build still refuses to clobber a tuned doctrine and now **warns when it differs** instead of reporting *"left untouched"* and nothing else.

    **(j) What this item does not claim.** Neither fix has been measured in the engine. C15's mechanism is established from the archived bodies and the shipped seed data, which is strong evidence about the **cause** and none at all about the **rate** after the fix. **A single run may open a question; it may not close one**, which is why the acceptance re-measurement that follows is specified as three or more pairs per model before it is run. Running total unchanged at **≈$2.57 of $5**.

42. **The re-measurement ran. Acceptance rose from 66.7 % to 86.2 % at 7B — and the same runs show the fix removed the rejection without removing the bad order. C15 REOPENS.** *(v1.8.26 — three 600 s paired `local` runs at `qwen2.5:7b-instruct-q8_0` on the post-C15/C16 build, 2026-08-06. **No network, no cost.** The 14B arm did not run; see (f).)*

    | 7B, post-fix | accepted / resolved | acceptance |
    |---|---|---|
    | 211824Z | 6 / 7 | 85.7 % |
    | 213840Z | 32 / 37 | 86.5 % |
    | 215855Z | 12 / 14 | 85.7 % |
    | **Pooled** | **50 / 58** | **86.2 %** |

    **(a) The rejection classes C15 and C16 are gone, and that part is unambiguous.** `reject.range` is **0 of 58**, against 7 of 27 in the 14B baseline. `reject.clamp` — *"cruiseSpeedMps 600 exceeds safety.maxSpeedMps 400"* — is **0 of 58 against 3 of 75** in the 7B baseline, and that class is the one mechanically connected to the speed anchor. `reasonTruncated` is **0**, as expected: C16 was a 14B behaviour and the 7B never approached the cap. The live smoke passes **20/20 in 3 of 3** (20 rather than 19 because this revision added the deployed-doctrine assertion), and latency is **1.8–9.5 s**.

    **(b) And then the accepted orders were read, which is the half a rate cannot show.** Commanded cruise speeds, before and after:

    | | commanded `cruiseSpeedMps` values |
    |---|---|
    | **Pre-fix** (56 accepted) | `250.0` ×49, `300.0` ×1, `400.0` ×6 |
    | **Post-fix** (50 accepted) | `319.99969775395874`, `318.9270822359112`, `1.50265015163732`, `1.5`, `12.75`, `123.927`, … |

    **A model does not spontaneously emit thirteen significant figures.** Pre-fix it typed round numbers; post-fix it is **copying a float out of the prompt**. The copied values fall into **three clusters — ≈320.0, ≈318.93, and ≈1.50** — which is exactly the signature of a model selecting among `own.speedMps`, `own.velE` and `own.velN` rather than reading the one it was given. One entity's run swings **320 → 1.5 → 318.93 across consecutive 20 s windows**, which no airframe does.

    **(c) So C15's fix corrected the sign and not the selection, and REOPENS on that narrower ground.** The suffix used to offer three numbers that look like speeds and now offers four. Adding `own.speedMps` guaranteed that a copied value is **positive**, which is why `range` and `clamp` went to zero — **and a positive wrong number is one the validator has no reason to refuse.** Pre-fix, a bad speed was **rejected and counted**; post-fix, a bad speed is **accepted and flown**. Part of the 19.5-point acceptance gain is a failure changing category rather than disappearing, and reporting the gain without this would be reporting the flattering half.

    **(d) Nothing anywhere bounds a commanded speed from below, and the asymmetry is visible in the config.** Stage A's A7 checks `> 0`. Stage B's B6 checks `cruiseSpeedMps > config.maxSpeedMps` and nothing else. `CommanderConfig` carries **`minAltitudeHaeM`** — a floor, because too low is dangerous — and **no `minSpeedMps`**, though an aircraft below its stall speed is not flying. A `1.5` m/s cruise order for a fighter passes both stages today. Opened as **C19**.

    **(e) Whether the `1.5` came from the snapshot or from the model cannot be determined from the order log** — the record carries `promptHash` and `snapshotHash` and no snapshot content. That is **C18's missing instrument**, and this is the second independent reason to want it inside one revision. C18 was speculative when it was opened; it is now load-bearing.

    **(f) The 14B arm is BLOCKED, not measured, and no 14B number is reported.** Two pairs were attempted and both produced **0 of 2 resolved orders**, every rejection `reject.transport` — *"no HTTP response … or the request exceeded 90 s"*. Measured cause: the model reports **15.75 GB** resident at **93 % on GPU / 7 % offloaded to CPU**, with the GPU at **16,002 of 16,376 MiB** and ~5.8 GB held by desktop processes. **This is not attributable to the prefix growth in item 41(h):** the 7B ran three clean pairs on the **same build with the same 9,642-byte prefix** at 1.8–9.5 s, and the four archived 14B baseline runs on this same host returned in **3.7–17.1 s**. A ~40× slowdown is a VRAM-residency cliff, not 226 tokens. **What that leaves is a host condition this document cannot control**, and the honest consequence is that item 40's 14B figures have no post-fix counterpart. Carried as **C20**. **C16's fix is therefore unmeasured in the engine** — it only ever fired at 14B.

    **(g) The baseline this compares against is not reproducible from this document, which is a defect in item 40.** Item 40's table names all four 14B runs by timestamp; its 7B row says *"3 pairs, 18/27, 66.7 %"* and names none. **Eight 7B runs are archived, and four different three-run subsets give exactly 18/27.** Pooling all eight gives **56/75 = 74.7 %**. So the honest statement of the gain is *86.2 % against a baseline somewhere between 66.7 % and 74.7 %*, and the imprecision is this document's fault rather than the measurement's. **Every run in this item is named above.**

    **(h) What the number will and will not carry.** At n = 58 the 95 % Clopper–Pearson interval on 50/58 is roughly **[75 %, 93 %]** — it **excludes the ≥ 95 % soak bar** and **straddles the ≥ 90 % live-smoke assertion**, so this does not establish that either bar is met. And two rejection classes moved for reasons this change does not explain and this item does not claim: `reject.shape` (C14's `hold` rule) fell **9 → 2**, and `fratricide` rose **0 → 5** — all five in a single run, all against `RedSAM_FireControlRadar`, the same *engage whatever is in the track list* tendency item 40(d) recorded against munitions, now aimed at its own SAM site and caught by B4 every time.

    **The answer to the question that motivated the run.** Was ~61 % mostly self-inflicted or genuinely the model? **Partly self-inflicted — and the acceptance metric overstates how much.** The classes this document caused are gone; the behaviour underneath one of them is not, it merely stopped being counted. **That is C17's thesis demonstrated on this project's own fix**, and it is a stronger argument for moving the bar onto the engine than anything in item 41. Running total unchanged at **≈$2.57 of $5**.

45. **The comparison this project exists to make had never been made, and it answers against the commander: it suppresses the entity's shooting by 87 %, scores nothing, and loses 20 of 22 aircraft where the control loses none.** *(v1.8.29 — re-analysis of **every archived paired run**, 2026-08-07. **No new run, no inference server, no network, no cost**; the logs were already on disk.)*

    **What was measured, and why it could have been measured at any point since Phase 1b.** Every paired run writes a commander-on and a commander-off engine log side by side. Those logs carry `Weapon spawned … owner <E> target <T>`, `Detonation: <munition> … target=<T>`, and `Warhead damage applied: source=<munition> target=<T> … state=destroyed`. **Kills attribute to the munition's owner**, resolved through the spawn line, because the warhead line names the weapon and not the shooter. Nothing else was needed. **The live-smoke harness has never asserted on, or reported, a single outcome quantity** — it checks acceptance, postures, frame cost, timeouts and reject rates, and never once asks whether the commanded aircraft did better.

    **The comparison is a DEPLOYMENT comparison, and it changes two variables at once. That has to be said before the numbers, not after them.** `run-live-scenario.ps1` restores the **shipped** `oppint_red_interceptor.lua` before the control arm (line 414), so the two arms are:

    - **ON** — the commander-aware Tier-1 script **plus** the commander;
    - **OFF** — the **shipped stock script**, commander disabled.

    **Script and commander move together.** That is a valid A/B of *what an operator would deploy* against *what ships today*, and it is **not** an isolation of the commander. The distinction is load-bearing here because the mechanism below turns out to sit partly in the script.

    **Restricted to the builds where the fire path demonstrably works** — post-C12, after the named-hardpoint fix of v1.8.22, because item 37 establishes that earlier launches drew no loadout slot — **11 paired runs across `qwen2.5:7b-instruct-q8_0` and `qwen2.5:14b-instruct-q4_K_M`:**

    | | **A** — shipped script | **B** — commander-aware + commander | **C** — commander-aware, commander **OFF** |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | runs | 11 | 11 | **1** |
    | Launches by the commanded aircraft | **30** (2.7/run) | **4** (0.36/run) | **0** |
    | Detonations from those launches | **15** | **0** | **0** |
    | Kills by the commanded aircraft | **0** | **0** | **0** |
    | Commanded aircraft destroyed | **0** | **20** of 22 | **2** of 2 |

    **Arm C is the whole of this item, and it was run precisely because arms A and B could not be told apart.** It is the commander-aware Tier-1 script with the commander **disabled** — no orders, and therefore **no inference server, no model, no network at all**. **It reproduces arm B.** Zero launches, zero detonations, both aircraft lost. **The language model is not what makes the commanded aircraft shoot less and die. The reference Tier-1 script is.**

    **(a) Engagement collapses — and the mechanism is in the SCRIPT, not only in the model.** Four launches against thirty (an **87 % reduction**) and zero detonations against fifteen. **`considerFiring` is reachable only on the posture path.** When no valid order is published, `ai_commander_interceptor.lua` takes `fallBackToWaypoints`, which calls `navigation.resumeWaypointFollowing` and **returns without ever reaching the fire logic**. So a commanded aircraft with no order in force **does not shoot at all**, by construction.

    **The mechanism is readable in the code, which is why arm C's n = 1 is not the weakness it looks like.** This is a structural claim confirmed by observation, not a rate estimated from a sample — the same category as item 41 reading `-220.0` out of four archived bodies. And **a second, accidental instance already existed**: run `221939Z`, the C20 transport-starved pair, had the commander **enabled and delivering zero orders** (4 requested, 2 `reject.transport`, 2 unresolved). Its commanded arm launched **0 times and lost 2 aircraft**. **Two independent runs — one deliberate, one accidental — in which the model contributed nothing and the outcome was identical to arm B.**

    **AIC-VAL-2 specifies this behaviour, so the defect is a design decision rather than a bug.** At `Released` the ladder's own text reads *"the reference script reads this as 'commander absent' and resumes waypoint following."* **Resuming waypoint following is all it does** — it does not resume *fighting*. The consequence nobody wrote down is that **the commander-aware script is strictly less capable than the shipped one whenever the commander is silent**, which includes every gap between orders, every rejected order, every timeout, and the entire run if the backend is down.

    **(b) Neither arm has ever scored a kill, and that bounds what (a) means.** ***(v1.8.34 — SUPERSEDED as of `20260808T135722Z`: a `RedSu35` munition has now destroyed a `BlueF16`, in the script-only arm that did not exist when this was written. §Corrections item 50(b). The sentence was true of every run in the archive at the time and the reasoning below still governs the twelve pairs it is about.)*** **No `RedSu35` munition has destroyed anything in any archived run, in either arm.** The control's fifteen detonations produced zero kills. So the control is not winning — **it is surviving by not being anywhere dangerous**, and "survives while achieving nothing" is a low bar. **The commanded arm clears neither half of it:** the same zero kills, and twenty losses.

    **(c) The losses are the part that is not close.** **20 of a possible 22** commanded aircraft destroyed with the commander on; **0 of 22** with it off, in **11 of 11** pairs. The one Blue loss in every run is `BlueF16_02`, killed by `RedSAM_Launcher` — **an uncommanded entity, identically in both arms** — so it is not a commander effect in either direction. **The pattern also holds on the hosted `claude-haiku-4-5` pair (C1, v1.8.15)**: both Su-35s destroyed with the commander on, both surviving with it off. It is not a property of the local model.

    **(d) One of item 40's figures is corrected, and it is a definitional error rather than an arithmetic one.** Item 40's table reads *"Control launches / hits — 2/1, 4/2, 2/1, 2/1"*. **The launch counts are exactly right** (10 control, 2 commanded across those four pairs; independently reproduced here). **The "hits" column counted *detonations*, not kills** — 5 detonations, **0 kills**. "Hits" reads as kills to any reviewer, and the difference is the whole finding: **a detonation that destroys nothing is not a hit in the sense the word carries.**

    **(e) This does NOT contradict H1, and it must never be quoted as if it did.** H1's signal is *"posture transitions a domain reviewer marks appropriate"*, and its verdict is scoped to exactly that. §Corrections item 37 and the H1 verdict itself both state that **no outcome claim is admissible** from these pairs. **That was correct and it remains correct.** What is new is that the outcome question was *answerable from the same logs the whole time and nobody asked it.* **The two findings belong side by side**: a reader who sees *"H1 — SUPPORTED"* in §Key hypotheses and stops there will form a materially wrong impression of what this system does to an aircraft.

    **(f) What this does not establish.** **One scenario**, one force laydown; arm C is **one run**, carrying the mechanism rather than a rate. The commanded aircraft die in a fight the stock script never joins, so *"gets aircraft killed"* and *"gets aircraft into contact"* are still not separated — arm C shows only that **whichever it is, the model is not causing it.** And nothing here says the commander **cannot** help: it says that on this scenario, with this reference script, **the script gives up more than the model adds**, and the model was never given a fair test because its Tier-1 partner stops fighting the moment it stops talking.

    **(g) The gap it exposes is a harness gap, not a model one.** §Success metrics measures cost, latency, acceptance, schema-rejection rate, frame cost, and reproducibility — **six metrics, none of which is an outcome.** A commander can therefore score green on every published metric while doing this. The live smoke should **report** launches, detonations, kills and losses per arm, on the same "report, don't bar" footing v1.7.5 gave acceptance; that is a harness change and needs no grant. Carried as **C21**.

    **The honest summary, because it is the sentence an owner will want.** **On the only scenario this project has measured, deploying the commander makes the entity shoot 87 % less, hit nothing, and die — and the cause is the reference Tier-1 script, not the language model.** Run the same script with the commander switched off and the result is the same or worse: **zero launches, both aircraft lost.** `ai_commander_interceptor.lua` stops fighting whenever no order is in force, by a design AIC-VAL-2 states explicitly and whose cost nobody had measured. **That is a fixable defect in this project's own reference script**, it is where the next hour of work belongs, and until it is fixed **no run of this system has ever given the language model a fair test.** Running total unchanged at **≈$2.57 of $5**.

46. **The open-issues review: four things this document had settled are moved, and the estimate in item 45's last sentence is optimistic by roughly a factor of eight.** *(v1.8.30, 2026-08-07. No network, no cost, no grant, no engine run — re-analysis of the whole archived log set plus eight controlled requests to a local inference server carrying no scenario state. `docs/open-issues-review.md` carries the working; this item carries the results that change a requirement.)*

    **(a) C21 has four mechanisms and item 45 priced one.** *(All four are readable off the source, which puts them in the mechanism category rather than the rate category; the one rate below is labelled.)* **①** `fallBackToWaypoints` returns before `considerFiring` — item 45, correct. **②** `considerFiring` appears at **exactly one call site**, in the `engage` branch; it is absent from `crank`, `hold`, `ingress`, `defend`, and the unknown-posture arm. **`crank` is the sharpest of these** — the posture exists to support a shot already in the air, and the shipped script cranks *between* launches, so an `engage → crank` sequence means the aircraft takes one shot and stops. **③** **All three rungs of the AIC-VAL-2 ladder are non-fighting**, and this document has never said so: rung 1 retains an order that is 63 % likely to be `hold`, **rung 2's standing order is `hold` with `weaponsTight` by specification**, and rung 3 resumes waypoints. Item 45 identified rung 3. **Fixing `fallBackToWaypoints` alone would leave rungs 1 and 2 intact.** **④** **There is no automatic defensive reflex.** The shipped script's *first* action every tick is `flyDefensiveIfThreatened` — *"Survival first: an inbound missile overrides every other consideration, including RTB"* — triggered by a **munition-kind** track inside `kThreatRangeM` = 15,000 m, reacting in one tick. The commander-aware script flies `defend` only when the model orders it, on a 20 s cadence plus a measured p50 of **3,476 ms** and p95 of **9,488 ms**. **An inbound AMRAAM crosses 15 km in about fifteen seconds.** §Non-goals says *"anything reactive — missile defeat, merge maneuvering, launch timing — stays in Tier 0/1 where it already works"*, and **the reference script does not implement the Tier-0/1 half of that sentence**: missile defeat is assigned to Tier 1 and then delegated to a 20-second model loop. **This, not the shooting deficit, is the most plausible loss mechanism, and it is currently unseparated from it.** A second defect rides with it: even when `defend` *is* ordered, the commander-aware script flees `getClosestHostileTrackById(entityId)` with **no kind filter** — the nearest hostile *anything*, which in a BVR merge is usually an aircraft rather than the missile.

    **The rate that scales ②, and it is a distribution and establishes no mechanism.** Across all twenty archived order logs, 158 accepted orders: `hold` **100 (63.3 %)**, `defend` 26 (16.5 %), `ingress` 15 (9.5 %), **`engage` 13 (8.2 %)**, `crank` 4 (2.5 %). Joined with ②, which is structural, the safe statement is that **the fire path is reachable from 8.2 % of the orders this system has ever accepted** — the aircraft cannot shoot during 92 % of the time it *is* under a valid order, not merely during the gaps. **And the reason `engage` is rare is not mysterious:** `data/doctrine.txt`'s POSTURE SELECTION block says *"Hold is the correct answer far more often than it feels."* The doctrine steers toward `hold`; the script cannot fight in `hold`. **Nobody wrote those two sentences in the same room.**

    **Two latent script defects found while reading it, neither implicated in the archived losses.** `firstLoadedHardpoint` selects the first rail with ammunition **regardless of range**, against a `kMissileRangeM` of 60,000 m that **matches no rail in the scenario** — `R77_BVR` reaches 45,000 m and `R73_IR` 12,000 m, and the shipped script's `selectHardpoint` picks by envelope. The four archived commanded launches all fell at 17.6–27.0 km and none exercised it, so it is latent rather than observed. And there is **no winchester egress**: the stock script flies home on an empty rail, the commander-aware script sets a note and waits for an order that may not come.

    **(b) C14 is diagnosed and it was never a rate. Numeric bounds are enforced by nothing, on either backend.** `reject.shape` is **the largest rejection class in the archive — 16 of 55 (29.1 %)**, of which 15 are `posture 'hold' requires orbitRadiusM > 0`. A controlled probe of the local decoder — eight requests, each carrying a `format` schema whose bound **forbids** the value the prompt explicitly asks for, temperature 0, seed 1 — establishes that the local constrained decoder enforces type, `required`, `enum`, `additionalProperties` and string length, and **does not enforce numeric `minimum` or `maximum` at all, in either direction, including a zero-width range.** The eighth case reproduces the exact archived failure on demand from the shipped four-branch schema: `{"posture":"hold","orbitRadiusM":0}`, a document satisfying **no branch** of the `oneOf`. **Confirmed on four models across three families** — `qwen2.5:7b-instruct-q8_0` (the shipped default), `llama3.1:8b`, `mistral:7b-instruct`, `qwen3:8b` — all emitting the same violating document.

    **So the four-branch encoding solves half of its own problem, and §Corrections item 15 says which half.** Item 15's mechanism is *"`targetEntityId` forced empty by a zero-length bound, `orbitRadiusM` forced to zero by a zero-width numeric range."* **The string half works. The numeric half does not, on the local decoder, and never has.** **And the hosted path cannot express the rule either**, by inspection of the projection: `pinToConst` converts a zero-width numeric range to `const`, which the API does enforce — but the hold branch's `{minimum: 1.0, maximum: 50000.0}` is **not** zero-width, so it survives `pinToConst` untouched and is then stripped whole by the unsupported-keyword removal. **There is no `const` equivalent for "greater than zero."** The conclusion, as strongly as the evidence allows: ***"a `hold` order requires `orbitRadiusM > 0`" is enforced by nothing, anywhere, except Stage A rejecting the whole order after the fact.*** It is the only rule in the schema with that shape — every other conditional rule is a forced-to-a-constant rule, and those all work.

    **Why the hosted soak measured 0/240, and it is not what item 20 read it as.** Not because the projection holds the rule — it cannot. The fixtures simply never produced a `hold` with radius 0. Item 20's *"the mechanical projection preserved the four-branch encoding's effect"* is **true for three of the four rules and false for this one**, and 0/240 is consistent with either explanation. **This is item 42(c)'s failure mode again: a distribution of outputs read as evidence of a mechanism.**

    **The cheapest remedy was tested and does not work.** Same schema, same adversarial prompt, prefixed with an explicit rule naming the field, the failure and the remedy value: `qwen2.5:7b-instruct-q8_0` **still violates**, as do `llama3.1:8b`, `mistral:7b-instruct` and `qwen3:8b`; only `qwen2.5:14b-instruct-q4_K_M` complies. The prompt was deliberately adversarial and this is one request per model rather than a rate, but it is sufficient for the decision: **a prompt line is not reliably sufficient on the shipped default model.** Note also that **`orbitRadiusM` is not mentioned anywhere in `data/doctrine.txt`** — the doctrine explains posture selection at length and never names the fields a posture must carry — so the model's only source for the rule was a JSON `description` attached to a keyword the decoder discards. **AIC-ORD-1 therefore repairs the field rather than rejecting the order**, on C16's precedent and with `safety.defaultOrbitRadiusM`, which AIC-VAL-2 rung 2 already uses for the same field in the same posture. **C14 CLOSES.**

    **One observation, labelled distributional and carrying nothing.** All 15 hold-radius rejections are on `RedSu35_02` and none on `RedSu35_01`, while `RedSu35_02` also produced 41 **accepted** `hold` orders; eight of the fifteen occurred at `serial: 1` with an identical response body across five runs on three days. **No mechanism is claimed from this.** Item 40's *"always on `RedSu35_02`"* was the symptom's address and not its cause, and the same caution applies.

    **(c) Fourteen of 55 rejections (25.5 %) are a discrimination the prompt structurally denies.** The prompt gives the model `{id, rangeM, snrDb}` per track and nothing else, and AIC-SEC-2 asserts exactly that. The doctrine then says, in READING THE SITUATION BLOCK: *"Nothing else is known: not the contact's type, not its team, not its heading. **Do not infer from an id what the id does not say.**"* **The only discriminator available is the one the doctrine forbids using, and Stage B then rejects the model for failing to discriminate** — 4 × `targetClass` (all munitions), 5 × `track` (all `*_wpn_*` ids naming munitions that had already detonated), 5 × `fratricide` (all `RedSAM_FireControlRadar`). **The doctrine and Stage B are in direct contradiction and the model is on the losing side of it.**

    **The fratricide case is airtight and it indicts Tier 1 rather than the model.** Stage B runs **B3 before B4**, so all five fratricide rejections **passed B3** — which means `RedSAM_FireControlRadar` **was in Tier 1's reported track list.** The commander-aware script's `reportTracks` forwards every sensor track unfiltered; the shipped script's `listHostileAirPlatforms` reads `entityControl.getEntityInfo(targetId)` and filters by team, kind and domain. **The team information is available in Lua, Tier 1 has it in hand, and the commander-aware script discards it before reporting.** The model was handed its own side's SAM radar as an indistinguishable contact and then rejected for naming it. **C13's close rejected filtering Tier 1's reports because it *"would blind `defend`"*, which is sound for munitions and does not apply at all to own-team contacts** — nothing in `defend` requires visibility of a friendly SAM radar. The three classes therefore split: **own-team contacts** are filtered in Tier 1, where the data already is; **munitions** stay visible per C13 and become *distinguishable* by widening the track row; **waypoint altitude 0** is a doctrine sentence naming the floor. §Out of scope's deferred row carries the revisit condition *"if order quality shows the model cannot discriminate targets without them"* — **it is met**, and `kind` and `team` are promoted while `domain` stays deferred. **The row's own stated cost — *"each added string is a new injection surface to charset-filter"* — does not apply to them, because both are enumerated scalars rather than free text.** ADR-6 is not violated: filtering own-team contacts out of a **sensor** picture, and reporting a **kind** the sensor track already carries, are Tier 1 reporting what it sees more precisely. Nothing is synthesised.

    **(d) The latency row has three entries and only one has ever been reported.** Computed from the archive for the first time this session: **`qwen2.5:7b-instruct-q8_0` in-engine (n = 115) runs p50 3,400 ms / p95 7,975 ms against a ≤ 20 s target — MET, with 60 % headroom.** The 14B runs p50 6,066 / p95 **17,109 ms**, which is not a target miss but is a control-loop margin of under three seconds against the 20 s cadence, on a model this project does not default to. **The shipped default backend meets its latency target comfortably and this document has never said so** — the row was written for CPU inference and is running on GPU. **The hosted target is not moved**: v1.3's rule stands, C10 established the cause is variance rather than a floor, and the cadence already absorbs a p99 of 7,099 ms. What changes is that the row states in its own text that the hosted entry is **not control-loop-binding**, which converts a permanently red row into a condition. **One thing genuinely open:** the variance is a provider property no prompt-side change touches, and this project has no retry-on-slow path — only a 90 s transport budget and a latest-wins slot. If the cadence is ever reduced, the remedy is a hedged request or a shorter budget with a retry, not a smaller prompt.

    **(e) Three figures were stale, and one of them is contaminated by C21.** Run `20260807T133621Z` was archived after item 45 and nobody folded it in: the post-C12 pairs become **12** (ON 4 launches / 0 detonations / 0 kills / **22 of 24 lost**; OFF 32 / 16 / 0 / **0 of 24**), and 87 % launch-suppression becomes 87.5 %. 7B post-fix acceptance moves **50/58 = 86.2 % → 59/70 = 84.3 % [73.6, 91.9]**; pooled post-fix **78/97 → 87/109 = 79.8 % [71.1, 86.9]**; the whole archive is 158/213 = 74.2 % [67.8, 79.9]. **No verdict moves.** The point is that §Success metrics' headline in-engine number was superseded by this project's own next run, which is precisely the staleness C17 is about. **And the contamination: 10 of 55 rejections (18.2 %) are `roster` — orders that resolved after the aircraft they were for had been destroyed.** They are not model failures in any sense; excluding them moves pooled acceptance from 74.2 % to **77.8 %**. **`roster` rejections can only occur when commanded aircraft die, and commanded aircraft die because of C21** — so the in-engine acceptance rate, the number C17 is a dispute about, is partly a function of the Tier-1 defect in (a), and that component will partly disappear when (a) is fixed.

    **The intervals above are 95 % Clopper–Pearson**, computed with an implementation validated against this document's own published figure — 50/58 → [74.6 %, 93.9 %] against v1.8.26's *"roughly [75 %, 93 %]"*. **In-engine acceptance SHALL be quoted as an interval from here on.** Every interval in play is 15–30 points wide, and quoting point estimates to one decimal (86.2 %, 71.8 %, 80.4 %) implies a precision the samples do not carry. **`84.3 % [74, 92]` cannot be misread as precise and cannot silently go stale in the way a bare decimal can**, which is how 86.2 % came to be quoted after its successor run existed. **Do not chase n:** a ±5-point interval needs roughly 250–400 resolved orders, twenty-five to forty paired runs, nine to fifteen hours of wall clock — and per (a) every one of those orders would be measured against a Tier 1 that stops fighting. **The n problem is downstream of the C21 problem and must not be attacked first.**

    **(f) The three unexercised changes are all confirmed unexercised, and one of them turns out to be load-bearing.** **`own.courseDeg` has never been sent to a model:** of twenty archived run directories, exactly one carries an `own` block at all, and that run's records carry **`headingDeg: 270.0` with `velE: -220.0`** — the *broken* field. Grep across the archive returns **zero** occurrences of `courseDeg`. **And the doctrine gap is larger than "never mentions the field":** `data/doctrine.txt` mentions `own.speedMps` three times with a whole CRUISE SPEED block, and `velN`/`velE`/`velD` explaining they are not speeds, and **names no heading or course field at all** — so the suffix has always carried a direction the doctrine never told the model how to read, and for the project's whole life that direction was wrong. **C16's truncation path has still never fired** (`reasonTruncated: 0` in all 16 stats records) **and the cap raise is doing measurable work anyway: 14 of 158 accepted orders carry a `reason` longer than 200 characters, so the raise admitted 14 orders the old cap would have rejected whole** — and per (a)③ each rejection would have left a stale order in force. **The observed maximum is 449 characters, 88 % of the new 512 cap**, which is closer than the derivation implies and is the number that decides whether 512 survives a model change. **C19's floor has fired exactly once** (`cruiseSpeedMps 1 is below safety.minSpeedMps 50`), which is the expected outcome on a much smaller post-fix sample and **is not evidence the check is unnecessary** — C19 was opened because *five* under-50 orders had been accepted before the floor existed. One caveat worth recording: item 44 established the copying was `own.speedMps` reported accurately, so the floor now guards a **snapshot-freshness** problem more than a model problem, and if snapshot freshness is ever fixed the floor may stop firing entirely. *"The floor rarely fires"* must not later be read as *"the floor is not needed."*

    **(g) Repository visibility is confirmed rather than assumed.** Checked 2026-08-07: **private.** The checklist box is ticked with a date. It is not paperwork — the repository holds `data/doctrine.txt`, the full order schema, this document's description of a proprietary platform's internals by component type and field path, and eight measurement CSVs, and **`tools/check-artifacts.ps1` is built entirely on the premise that the repository is the safe side of the boundary.** Had the answer been public, that guard would have been protecting the wrong thing. **The other governance box is unchanged and is not this document's to tick:** all six grants authorize measurement, so there is no authorization under which an operator other than the measurer may turn the hosted backend on. **One dependency this item adds to it:** widening the track row per (c) changes what leaves the machine, so **AIC-SEC-2 and `docs/egress.md` change before any hosted request under the new field set**, and any standing grant must postdate that change. Granting against today's field set and then widening it is exactly the inference §Tenet 4's gate exists to prevent.

    **(h) Found in passing, and small.** The **deployed doctrine is 892 bytes behind the repository's** — exactly C15's CRUISE SPEED block — and the build warns about it on every build. **The archived runs are unaffected**, because the smoke harness copies the repository copy in, asserts the sizes match, and restores the operator's in its `finally`; but any *interactive* run uses the stale block, and a warning that fires every time will be ignored eventually. **Three different denominators are in use for `reject.shape`** — item 39(d)'s 12.5 %, and the pooled archive's 16 of 55 rejections or 16 of 213 resolved orders. All are defensible; none states its denominator in the same sentence. And **run `20260806T223956Z` contains only an `orders-previous-run` file**, invisible to both analysers, so the archive's directory count (21) overstates the usable runs (20).

    **(i) What the doctrine and prompt changes cost, derived rather than measured, and labelled as derived.** The doctrine grows **7,824 → 9,782 bytes** and the rendered prefix **9,642 → 11,600** — four paragraphs naming the two new track attributes, `own.courseDeg`, the waypoint altitude floor, and the orbit-radius rule. **The direction is the safe one:** the cached block moves **further above** Haiku 4.5's 4,096-token minimum, not toward it — ≈2,933 prefix tokens plus the structural schema copy gives ≈**5,839** cached tokens against ≈5,344 before, a margin of ≈**1,743 tokens (42.6 %)** where it was ≈1,248 (30.5 %). The hazard `PromptRendererTests.cpp` guards is a prefix *shrinking* under the minimum silently; growth cannot trigger it. **The marginal cost is ≈+495 cached tokens per order** — at Haiku's $1/MTok input and the 0.1× cache-read rate, **≈+$0.00005 per order, ≈+$0.04 per four-ship scenario-hour**, taking §Cost model's $0.88 to roughly **$0.92** against a ≤ $1.10 target. **Every figure in this paragraph is arithmetic on a measured byte count, not a new measurement**, and §Cost model's rows are left on the numbers that were actually measured — the difference between derived and measured is what §Corrections exists to keep visible, and item 33(c) is this document's record of what happens when it stops being. The two new track fields also widen the **volatile suffix** by ~40 bytes per track, which is uncached and therefore charged at 1×; at eight tracks that is under 100 tokens an order and is inside the rounding of the figure above.

    **(j) `docs/summary.md` exists, and it is gated rather than merely written.** This document is **4,000 lines**, and it is not readable by an owner: its most important finding sits at line 859 in a section called *"Corrections verified in-tree."* The concrete evidence that this is a real problem rather than a stylistic complaint is (e) above — **§Success metrics is where a reader looks for the verdict, and its in-engine acceptance figure was one run stale**, under a subsection describing why that number needed watching. A document its own maintainers cannot keep synchronised across 4,000 lines needs a shorter front door. Three properties, learned from exactly what went stale here: **it carries no number that is not also in this document**, so there is one place a figure can be wrong; **it is regenerated at each phase close rather than maintained continuously**, because this project has now demonstrated twice that continuously-maintained duplicate figures drift; and **it leads with the outcome finding** rather than with the metric table, so an owner who reads only the first paragraph learns that the system made the entity worse and that the cause was fixable and local. **`tools/lint-prd.ps1` gained a tenth check** asserting that the summary's version stamp matches this document's Status line — **so a stale summary fails the gate instead of being discovered by a reader**, which is the failure mode the summary exists to prevent and would otherwise reproduce one file over.

    **What item 46 is worth, in one sentence.** The project has built a careful, well-instrumented pipeline and has never once measured whether it helps; when it finally did, the answer was no — **and the reason is in this project's own deterministic tier**, which means no run to date has given the language model a fair test, and **the acceptance, order-quality and latency questions downstream are all measured against a crippled Tier 1.** Running total unchanged at **≈$2.57 of $5**.

47. **The fixed script ran. The arm that had never existed says the fix works, the commander is measurably neutral on one run, and the fix made a second defect visible that the first one had been hiding.** *(v1.8.31, 2026-08-08. No network, no cost, no grant; one three-arm 600 s `local` run at `qwen2.5:7b-instruct-q8_0`, archived at `20260808T095026Z-local`. Live smoke: **22 checks, 0 failed**.)*

    **(a) The outcome table, and the comparison that carries the finding.**

    | Arm | launches | detonations | kills | aircraft lost |
    |---|---|---|---|---|
    | **ON** — commander-aware script + commander | **3** | **2** | 0 | **0 of 2** |
    | **SCRIPT-ONLY** — commander-aware script, commander OFF, no model *(first ever)* | **3** | **2** | 0 | **0 of 2** |
    | **OFF** — shipped `oppint_red_interceptor.lua` | 2 | 1 | 0 | 0 of 2 |
    | *item 45's arm C — the **broken** script, commander OFF, no model* | *0* | *0* | *0* | ***2 of 2*** |
    | *item 46(e)'s twelve ON pairs — the **broken** script + commander* | *4 total* | *0* | *0* | ***22 of 24*** |

    **The load-bearing comparison is the fourth row against the second, and it is load-bearing because it is the only one in this document that changes exactly one thing.** Same scenario, same laydown, same commander state (off), no model in either — **only the reference script differs.** Arm C: **0 launches, 2 of 2 lost.** The fixed script: **3 launches, 2 detonations, 0 of 2 lost**, and both aircraft end the run in `engage (BlueF16_01, no order)` — fighting, with nothing commanding them. Every other pairing in this project moves two variables at once, which is the error item 45(b) had to correct about itself.

    ***"Does the uncommanded script ever fire?"* is a mechanism readable directly off recorded values**, which is the one category §Scope authority's fourth rule lets a single run close. It was 0 across a whole run and is now 3. **C21 CLOSES on that mechanism.**

    **What C21's close explicitly does NOT include.** C21's row has two clauses — the script *stops fighting*, and it *costs the entity the engagement*. **The first is fixed and demonstrated. The second is a rate and one run does not carry it.** 0 of 2 lost against a historical 22 of 24 is a single sample, and the twelve pairs behind the historical figure took eleven runs more than this. **No outcome rate is claimed here, and the launch counts are not compared to the shipped script's** — the fixed script's 3 against stock's 2 is well inside what one run of a stochastic scenario produces either way.

    **C22 CLOSES.** Its question was whether the arm exists and what it says. It exists, it ran, and it says the script fights.

    **(b) The commander is measurably neutral, on one run, and that is the whole of it.** The commander-on and script-only arms are **identical: 3 / 2 / 0 / 0 on every column.** This is **the first unconfounded commander comparison this project has ever made** — the ON/OFF pair swaps the mission script as well, which is exactly what item 45(b) had to retract. **It settles nothing in either direction and is recorded so the identity cannot later be quoted as one.** A null at n = 1 is not evidence that the commander does nothing; it is one run in which it did not visibly change the columns this analyser counts. **And still zero kills in every arm**, unchanged across the entire archive: no `RedSu35` munition has ever destroyed anything.

    **(c) Three fixes reach the field for the first time, and all three are the category a single run settles.** **`own.courseDeg` varies** — **20 distinct values across 30 samples on `RedSu35_02`**, against `headingDeg`'s **one distinct value across fourteen samples, spread 0.000** — and it agrees with the velocity it is derived from (course 97.5° at `velN` −28.8 / `velE` +218.1). Item 46(f) established the corrected field had **never been sent to a model**; it has now. **`reject.shape` is 0 of 38 requested**, where it was **the largest rejection class in the archive at 16 of 55**, and **`orbitRadiusRepaired` fired once** — C14's repair works on the product rather than only in the adversarial corpus. Each of these is a *"does this number ever change?"* question, which is the example §Scope authority's fourth rule gives.

    **(d) C23 OPENS: an uncommanded aircraft that runs out of route stops flying, and every order after that is rejected for copying its own stopped speed.** Acceptance on this run was **16 of 37 resolved**, and **all 21 rejections are one thing** — `cruiseSpeedMps` below `safety.minSpeedMps`, every one of them on `RedSu35_02`. **The model is not at fault and the record proves it:** item 44 established the model copies `own.speedMps` exactly, and the snapshot shows `own.speedMps` collapsing to **4.274** at t=180.4 and then sitting at **exactly 1.5** with `velN` 0.1 and `velE` 1.5 for the remainder of the run. The model emitted `4.274373306340072` and then `1.5`. **It reported what it was shown.**

    The chain is readable in the mission log: the model ordered **`hold`** → `RedSu35_02` came off the fight → it lost the track picture → the order expired → `waypoints (no order, no contact)` → `resumeWaypointFollowing` with an exhausted route → **stationary for roughly 400 seconds.**

    **The stall path is not new, and that is the interesting part.** The pre-v1.8.30 script's `fallBackToWaypoints` called the same verb in the same situation. What is new is that **the aircraft survives long enough to sit in it**: previously it was destroyed first. **C19's floor fired once in the entire prior archive and 21 times in this single run** — the same defect, made visible by removing the one that had been masking it. Item 46(f) recorded the possibility in advance: *"the floor now guards against a snapshot freshness problem more than a model problem."* This is that, arriving.

    **It is carried rather than fixed, because the layer is a genuine choice and picking one now would be picking it blind.** The remedies sit in three places and they are not equivalent: **the script** could refuse to hand a stationary aircraft to `resumeWaypointFollowing`, or fly a holding pattern instead; **the doctrine** could say that `hold` away from the picture is how an aircraft leaves a fight it cannot rejoin; **the snapshot** could decline to offer a stalled own-speed as a cruise-speed anchor at all. The first is the smallest change and the third is the one that addresses what item 44 actually measured. **No acceptance rate is quoted from this run** — 16 of 37 is one aircraft's stall wearing a rate's name, and §Success metrics' interval rule applies.

    **(e) `docs/egress.md` was found stale on three counts and is corrected in this revision.** The page that exists to state exactly what leaves the machine was last revised **2026-08-05** and the prompt changed three times after it: **`own.speedMps`** added v1.8.25, **`own.headingDeg` replaced by `own.courseDeg`** v1.8.28, and **the track row widened with `kind` and `team`** v1.8.30 — while the document asserted, in its own words, *"the field list above is exhaustive and has not changed."* It also claimed the reporting verbs accept *"numbers only"*, which was **never** true: `targetEntityId`, `hardpointName` and `weaponProfileName` are strings and always have been. **None of the three widened the trust boundary** — the two `own.*` fields are arithmetic on components already on the list, and the track attributes are closed enums that cannot carry a value outside their vocabulary — **and nothing leaked: no hosted request has ever been made under any of the three field sets**, verified rather than assumed by enumerating the archive, which holds **22 run directories and not one hosted run**. **But an owner authorizing egress against that page would have been authorizing against a list that was not the list**, which is the single failure that document exists to prevent. Recorded here rather than quietly corrected, and it is worth noting that **v1.8.30's own review asserted the file "is maintained against the adapter as implemented" without checking** — the claim and its refutation are three days apart in the same project.

    **What this item is worth, in one sentence.** The defect that made every downstream measurement suspect is fixed and demonstrated on the arm built to test it — **and the first thing the fix revealed is that the aircraft had been dying before anyone could see it stop flying.** Running total unchanged at **≈$2.57 of $5**.

48. **Two Haiku latency samples have been quoted as one number since v1.8.20, and v1.8.30 made it worse by giving the composite a sample size.** *(v1.8.32, 2026-08-08. No run, no network, no cost. **No verdict moves:** the latency row read MISSED before and reads MISSED after, under either sample.)*

    **(a) There are two measurements and they are different samples.** The **240-order Phase 2 soak** (v1.8.4, `claude-haiku-4-5`, six synthetic fixtures) measured **p50 2,602 / p95 4,615 / p99 7,099 ms**. **C10's 48-order arm** (v1.8.20, sixth grant, same fixtures, regenerated bodies) measured a **total p95 of 7,238 ms**. Both are real, neither is wrong, and **they were never one distribution** — 7,238 exceeds the soak's own p99, which is arithmetically impossible within a single sample and is the tell nobody read.

    **(b) v1.8.20 attributed C10's number to a section that does not contain it.** Its text reads *"§Success metrics still reads MISSED at a total p95 of 7,238 ms."* **§Success metrics has read 4,615 ms since v1.8.4 and still does.** The sentence was describing this document incorrectly, in a revision whose whole subject was a latency figure, and it stood for eleven revisions.

    **(c) v1.8.30 compounded it rather than catching it, and the compounded form is worse.** Its new latency row read *"Haiku 4.5 p50 2,602 / p95 7,238 ms (n = 240)"* — **a p50 from the soak and a p95 from C10's arm, presented under a single sample size.** The inherited error was a misattribution; this one manufactures a statistic that was never computed and **dresses it in an `n`**, which is the property that makes it read as more settled than the thing it replaced. The row now names both samples separately.

    **(d) The mechanism is one this document has already recorded twice, arriving in a third costume.** Item 20 read a 0/240 as evidence of a mechanism the projection could not hold; item 42(c) read a cluster of floats as field-selection. Both were **a figure carried forward by quotation rather than by re-derivation**, and each restatement made it look more established. **This one was found by re-deriving a number for a README** — which is the only reason it was found at all, and is an argument for the practice rather than for the README.

    **(e) `README.md` is rewritten, and it was the staler of the two front doors.** It reported **Phase 2 as "not started"** when Phase 2 had run, been measured at **$1.05** per four-ship scenario-hour, been exercised in-engine, and spent six egress grants. It carried **98/98** in prose and **87** in its own table against a real **156**; **30** in prose and **25** in the table against a real **30**; and **17** live checks against **22**. And it led with C5's memorised-coordinate finding as *"the phase's most useful finding"* — **a bounded negative at n = 11** — while **C21, the largest result this project has produced, appeared nowhere in it.** An owner reading it would conclude the hosted path was never attempted and that the project's headline result is an anecdote about Perth.

    **Why it drifted and `docs/summary.md` will not.** The summary carries a version stamp that `tools/lint-prd.ps1` pins to this document's Status line, so a stale summary **fails the gate**. The README had no such pin and no such gate. **It still does not** — pinning prose to a version number is the wrong instrument for a document that is mostly build instructions, and the honest control is that it is regenerated at each phase close alongside the summary. Recorded here so the next reader knows which of the two front doors is machine-checked and which is not. Running total unchanged at **≈$2.57 of $5**.

49. **Three of the five rows this document called "open" were dormant, and the register had no way to say so.** *(v1.8.33, 2026-08-08. No run, no network, no cost, no grant, no engine, no inference server. **No verdict moves and no measured figure changes:** this revision closes one row on a mechanism already in the record, defers two, and adds a state to a table.)*

    **(a) The register recorded two states and needed three.** §Carried out of Phase 3 has been this project's single open-item register since v1.8.17, and it marks a row **closed** by striking the id through and writing a dated result into the `Blocked on` cell — and **open** by doing neither. So *"open"* has been carrying two incompatible meanings at once: *a live question someone should answer*, and *a dormant row nobody should touch*. **At v1.8.32 the table read five open rows when the honest answer was two.** The column is headed **"Blocked on"** and **not one of C8, C5 or C6 was blocked on anything a person could go and do** — each cell held a destination. **This is a MECHANISM, readable off the document itself**; it needs no run, no sample and no interval, and it is the kind of defect that survives precisely because every individual row is accurate. Fixed by specifying **OPEN / DEFERRED / CLOSED** under the register, with the rule that a **DEFERRED row SHALL carry a revisit condition a reader can test without running anything, and SHALL state what work that condition then triggers.** A deferral naming no condition is an aspirational deferral, which is invisible debt — the failure `tools/lint-prd.ps1`'s open-question check exists to catch, and the reason OQ-4 aged three revisions past its decision target unnoticed.

    **(c) C8 is DEFERRED, and a close was considered and refused.** Its position is stated — `claude.maxTokens = 512` is right for the shipped default and **no other value is derivable from the data this project holds**, because 673 is a *sample* maximum from a run whose per-fixture means move by up to 71 tokens (item 27(e)). **Its revisit condition is that a non-Haiku model is proposed as `claude.model`'s default**, testable against one line of AIC-API-2. **A close was refused because a close asserts nothing further is ever required, and that is false here:** if a non-Haiku default is proposed, the ceiling must be re-measured over **at least two independent runs** — one run cannot separate a sample maximum from a bound, which is the entire content of the row — and it **SHALL NOT** be scaled from another model's headroom, a method v1.8.6 declined and measurement then vindicated at ~2,000 against a real 673. **Closing the row would have deleted the only place that instruction lives as a live obligation.**

It answers no roadmap question.
