53. **C23's fix is implemented — and the re-derivation that had to precede it refutes two of this document's own statements about C23, one of which changed how the fix had to be written.** *(v1.8.37, 2026-08-09. **No run, no network, no cost, no grant, no engine, no inference server.** Re-derivation of the whole archived order set and of the three 2026-08-08 mission logs, plus a Lua change and six offline tests. **The consolidated argument is `docs/c23-report.md`**, which is written to be read without this document open; this item carries only what changes a requirement or a claim.)*

    **(a) The fix is in, and it is falsified rather than merely asserted.** AIC-ORD-2 clauses 7 and 8 are implemented in `lua/ai_commander_interceptor.lua`, with **six new tests in `tests/ReferenceScriptTests.cpp` — 162/162.** Run against the **pre-fix** script with the tests unchanged, **three of the six fail**: clause 7's, the eight-case clause 8 regression driven at the archived stall velocity (`velN 0.0544, velE 1.4990, velD 0.0`), and the hysteresis band. **The other two pass before and after by design** — they pin the boundary the fix must not cross and the unreadable-velocity case — and that distinction is recorded because *"every new test fails on the old code"* is a property worth wanting and not one worth faking. **No revision was required to write the code**: both clauses landed in v1.8.36 and nothing implemented goes beyond them, which is §Scope authority working in the direction it was written for.

    **(b) The speed echo is universal, and this document had only ever established it for one posture.** Across **every accepted order in the archive that can be joined to the snapshot it answered — 61 of 61 — `cruiseSpeedMps` equals `own.speedMps` to the last bit of a double**: `defend` 25, `hold` 19, `engage` 13, `ingress` 4. **So an order's speed is the aircraft's own current speed handed back to it. It can re-command a stall and can never break one.** That is the whole basis of clause 8's *"never to a speed read from an order"*, and until now it rested on item 44's nine samples on one posture. **It also disposes of the escape hypothesis in item 50(d)** — see (f). **The model remains exonerated, and more completely than the record says:** `data/doctrine.txt` does not merely permit the echo, it **instructs** it — *"start from the speed the aircraft is already making … re-issuing the current speed is always a defensible answer."*

    **(c) Item 51(b) is REFUTED: there is an arrival, and the aircraft has somewhere to fly.** Its text reads *"the aircraft is ordered to hold where it already is, **has nowhere to fly**, and coasts 320 → ~128 → 1.5000 m/s."* Measuring each 20 s sample's distance to the waypoint of the `hold` **actually in force at that moment**, the aircraft **ranges 3.2–4.4 km out and sustains 320.0000 m/s for up to sixty seconds under the same order, with no decay whatever.** The collapse begins in the **first 20 s sample after the aircraft is inside that order's `orbitRadiusM`** — **4 of 4** — and it is a loss of roughly **8 m/s²**, which is not a coast. **The intermediate value is run-specific** (128.0, 125.0, 6.555, 4.274); what replicates exactly is the endpoint, **52 samples at 1.5000**.

    **(d) And the archive contains a discriminator, which is why this is not a correlation across five outcomes.** **Twice the aircraft did not move at all.** In `095026` a `hold` at `orbitRadiusM` 1,000 left the aircraft **3,252.7 m outside** at 320.0000 m/s; **17.1 s after a new `hold` enlarged the radius to 8,000 — same position, same speed — it read 4.274 m/s.** In `135722` three `hold` orders at radius 1,000 held the aircraft **outside for sixty seconds at 320.0000 m/s**; **16.5 s after a radius-8,000 order put it inside, it read 6.555 m/s.** **The variable that moved is a field of the order document; the aircraft was not touched.** That separates *"a `hold` is in force"* — true for sixty seconds without a collapse — from *"inside the ordered radius"*. **What this does NOT establish is why**, and this item does not guess: the engine is closed-source in this tree, and the claim stops at the observable — **the ordered `cruiseSpeedMps` is not maintained once the aircraft is inside the ordered orbit.**

    **(e) That changed the implementation, so it is a finding rather than a footnote.** Clause 7 keys on *"where the ordered waypoint lies within the ordered `orbitRadiusM` of the aircraft's **current position**"*. **Read as a test at order-issue time** it fires on 19 of 19 archived holds and **misses a distant hold flown in entirely**. **Read as a per-tick test on the current distance — which is what "current position" says — it fires exactly where (c) and (d) put the pathology**, including on a hold flown in from 55 km, at the moment of capture. **The implementation is per-tick**, and both readings are pinned by tests: one asserts the script computes the orbit inside the radius, the other asserts it leaves a 55 km hold to the engine with the ordered radius unaltered.

    **(f) Item 50(d)'s two "survivors" were never exposed, and its escape hypothesis is superseded rather than confirmed.** Read off the reference script's own `setMode` lines rather than off the order log: `RedSu35_02` was in `hold` **mode** for **~320, ~360 and ~360 s** in the three runs and collapsed in all three; `RedSu35_01` was in it for **~20 s** twice and **never entered it at all** in the third, and collapsed in none. **Against a measured onset delay of 16.5–17.1 s, a 20 s exposure is not a counter-instance — it is an under-exposed case**, which removes the only evidence this archive contained against the onset claim. **There is no archived instance of a `hold` flown inside its own orbit radius for more than one cadence window that did not end at 1.5000 m/s: 3 of 3.** And what pulled the survivors out was not *"a new accepted order"* — by (b) a new order can only re-command the speed the aircraft already has. **Both passed to `defend (ordered)`, whose branch reads `flyDefend(entityId, kDefendSpeedMps)` and discards the ordered speed outright**, and stayed there for the last **490 s** of both runs. **Zero archived below-floor samples were taken under `defend`.** **This is offered at exactly that strength and NOT as a finding:** the discarded-speed half is one line of source, the outcome half is **n = 2 aircraft-runs** with obvious confounds — the same aircraft was also under munition threat and in a different part of the fight. **No rate is claimed and none is available.** It is recorded because it is clause 8's own rule, operating by accident, in the one posture that already implemented it.

    **(g) AIC-VAL-2 rung 2 specifies the defect, and nothing could ever have caught that.** The standing order is *"`posture=hold` … waypoint at the entity's position at expiry"* — **a hold at zero distance, written down as a requirement**, with `cruiseSpeedMps` inherited from the last accepted order and therefore, by (b), the speed the aircraft was already making. `FallbackLadder.cpp` implements it exactly. **27 of the 58 archived below-floor samples were taken at this rung.** **So without clause 7 the ladder re-creates C23 with no language model in the loop at all.** **The code matched the specification, so no divergence check could have found it** — which is the mirror image of item 50(e), where the code lagged a specification and a passing test defended the old behaviour. **AIC-VAL-2 now records the dependency and AIC-ORD-2's `hold` row now carries clause 7's qualification**, because the table row read as an unconditional instruction to call the verb clause 7 forbids. **No behaviour changes in this revision**; both edits make the document say what the code already does.

    **(h) Three quoted figures do not reproduce, and they are corrected here rather than in place.** ① *"39 of 39 samples below `safety.minSpeedMps`, across three runs and two aircraft"* (item 50(c)): there are now **58 samples across four runs — 46 under `hold`, 12 under no order at all.** The 39 was the two runs available at v1.8.34; ***"three runs" was two, and "two aircraft" was one*** — **every below-floor sample in the entire archive is on `RedSu35_02`.** Item 51(d)'s 45/12 reproduces exactly for the three 2026-08-08 runs; the fourth run adds one `hold` sample. ② *"19 of 19 archived `hold` orders"*: **19 of the 19 that are measurable, out of 114 archived holds.** The other 95 sit in runs whose `order.requested` records carry no `own` block, so they are **unmeasurable, not compliant** — item 51(a) says *"four runs carrying `own` blocks"* and is careful, but the headline and `docs/summary.md` read as a total, and **83 % of archived holds carry no evidence either way.** ③ *"the only hold beyond 10 km sits at t = 600.1"* (item 50(d)): **not reproducible.** Joining each accepted order's waypoint to the `own` block of the request it answered, **no accepted order anywhere in the measurable archive is more than 11.0 m from own position** — the 11.0 m being the residual of the model rounding own position to two decimals on three `ingress` orders. The figure most likely came from the same analysis that produced item 50(d)'s refuted claims; **recorded rather than quietly dropped**, per this section's convention.

    **(i) What this revision deliberately does not do, because the omissions are decisions.** **It does not close C23.** What closes is the specified fix; what remains is a **~5-minute confirming run** (specified in `docs/c23-report.md` §10.2 and **not** run here — nothing in the fix is blocked on it), the **doctrine correction still owed from item 52(f)**, and the owner's view on **five judgement calls** made inside clauses 7–8's licence and listed in the report's §7.3. **The doctrine correction was deliberately not taken:** it is not part of clauses 7–8, and it is coupled — `kShippedDoctrineBytes` in `tests/PromptRendererTests.cpp` pins the file's byte size and `CacheGuardTests.cpp` pins the prefix's cache eligibility — so it is a three-file change to the transmitted prompt and belongs in its own commit. **One new argument about it is recorded and is not acted on:** by (b) the doctrine currently *instructs* the echo, so the available change is **deleting an instruction rather than adding a prohibition**, which is not the intervention item 52(f)'s reasoning rejected and does not depend on the model obeying anything. **It is still not a fix** — the model may echo regardless — so it replaces nothing and clauses 7 and 8 stand either way. **And it quotes no new acceptance or latency figure:** no run was made, so the sentinel is unchanged. Running total unchanged at **≈$2.57 of $5**.

54. **C23's confirming run was made. It answers both open questions, it demonstrates a claim this document had only argued, and it found a defect in the fix that nothing offline could have found.** *(v1.8.38, 2026-08-09. Two local runs of "Mariana Shield" — ~2 minutes each — driving `tools/c23-hold-probe.lua` via `tools/run-c23-probe.ps1`, archived `20260809T102936Z-c23-probe` and `20260809T104112Z-c23-probe`. **The commander is not merely unconfigured but ASSERTED OFF**: the harness refuses to start if `data/config/plugins/ai-commander.cfg` exists, so `aiCommander` is nil throughout and no result below can be an artifact of a published order. **No inference server, no network, no cost, no grant.** The release tree is restored byte-for-byte in a `finally` block. Full working in `docs/c23-report.md` §10.2.)*

    **(a) The instrument, and why it is not a Tier-1 script.** `tools/c23-hold-probe.lua` implements no requirement, reads no order, never fires and never defends. It drives `navigation` directly from simulation time and logs `entityControl.getVelocityNed` and `getPositionGeodetic` at **1 Hz**, which is the whole point: the archive samples at the 20 s order cadence, and every timing statement C23 has ever made was bracketed by that. **This is the injection §Corrections item 51(f) said the question required** — *"no number of further runs will produce the counter-instance; it would have to be injected"* — and it is exactly as cheap as that item implied.

    **(b) Q1 is answered: a `hold` ordered FAR from the aircraft stops it too, and the trigger is the orbit boundary rather than the waypoint.** Ordered **20 km away**, `orbitRadiusM` 5,000, `cruiseSpeedMps` 320. Both aircraft held **320.0000 m/s for fifty seconds while outside the radius** — distance 21,123 → 5,260 m, no decay at any sample. At **t = 61.2 the aircraft is 5,260 m out and outside; at t = 62.1 it is 4,972 m out and inside; at t = 63.0 it reads 302.0000.** The deceleration is a clean **−20 m/s²** to about 42 m/s and then an exponential approach to the **1.5000** latch. **So the archive's 16.5–17.1 s onset delay was entirely an artifact of its 20 s sampling — the real delay is under one second**, and the 0 m echo determines *when* the collapse starts, not *whether*. **A replication rather than a coincidence:** the probe reads **4.2744 m/s** at t = 79.0 where archived run `095026` reads `own.speedMps` **4.274373306340072** at t = 180.4 — the same curve at the same point, with a language model in one and not the other. **The damage confound is ruled out off the record:** the only detonations against either Su-35 occur at t ≈ 85 and t ≈ 149, after the collapse.

    **(c) And that is what makes clause 7's PER-TICK reading load-bearing rather than a preference.** Item 53(e) argued the per-tick test from the clause's own *"current position"* wording and from a two-run natural experiment. **This run is the case the argument was about:** a hold whose waypoint is 20 km away is not within `orbitRadiusM` of the aircraft at order-issue time, so **an issue-time test would have handed it straight to `requestHoldPosition` and the aircraft would have stopped.** The per-tick test takes the geometry on the same sample the deceleration would otherwise have begun on.

    **(d) Q2 is answered: the recovery is ACHIEVED, not merely commanded — and this is the caveat that was keeping C23 open.** From exactly **1.5000 m/s**, `requestGoTo` to a point 25 km ahead at 300 m/s — precisely what the fixed reference script issues while recovering — put both aircraft above `safety.minSpeedMps` in **3.1 seconds** (23.5000 at +1.2 s, 42.5000 at +2.2 s, **60.5000 at +3.1 s**) and to 299.96 within twenty. The acceleration is **+20 m/s²**, the exact mirror of the deceleration. **AIC-ORD-2 clause 8's criterion asks for one cadence window and got 3.1 s of 20.** The wording-versus-instrument gap that `docs/c23-report.md` §9.2 records is **not** thereby fixed — the offline suite will still only ever assert the command — but the criterion is now satisfied in fact on two aircraft.

    **(e) A claim this document had only argued is now demonstrated: rung 2's geometry stalls an aircraft by itself.** The probe's first phase issues `requestHoldPosition` at the aircraft's **own position** — AIC-VAL-2 rung 2's published waypoint, and the order the model echoes — with **no model and no commander anywhere in the loop**. Result: **220.0000 m/s at t = 0.1, 1.5000 by t = 23.1, latched.** Item 53(g) inferred this from the specification and the code; this is the behaviour itself. **Without clause 7, a backend outage alone would produce C23.**

    **(f) The run found a defect IN THE FIX, and this is the strongest argument for having made it.** After peaking at 299.98 under a *continuing* 300 m/s command, both aircraft **settle at 132.2–146.5 m/s**. The archive corroborates it from the other direction: `RedSu35_01` flew `defend (ordered)` for 490 s under a commanded 320 and held about 150. **`kResumeFlyingSpeedMps` — the threshold at which the recovery latch clears — was 150.0, which sits INSIDE that band.** In normal flight the latch might therefore never have cleared: Tier 1 would have held navigation for the rest of the run, `hold` would never have orbited and `resumeWaypointFollowing` would never have run. The value had been chosen as *"half of Tier 1's cruise"* and had nothing else behind it. **It is now 100.0** — 2× the floor, so the entry/exit pair cannot chatter, and ~24 % clear of the lowest observed settling speed — **and a new assertion at 132.2 m/s pins the ceiling**, so a future raise back into the band fails a test rather than silently latching. **Neither the offline suite nor the archive could have found this**, and it is the one thing in C23's whole history that only a run could produce.

    **(g) The doctrine correction owed since item 52(f) is taken, and it turned out to be two sentences.** ① *"A value at or below zero, or one beyond the airframe's configured limit, is rejected outright"* — false since v1.8.27. The replacement states **the shape and deliberately not the number**: *"a value below the configured minimum … the minimum is not zero … the exact bound is a deployment setting."* **Writing `50` into a cacheable block that nothing keeps in step with `safety.minSpeedMps` would re-create this defect the next time an operator lowers it** — which `CommanderConfig.h` explicitly instructs a rotary-wing deployment to do — so a number would have been the same error with a fresher value. ② *"Re-issuing the current speed is **always** a defensible answer"* — **measurably false**: 61 of 61 accepted orders took that advice and 58 were rejected for it. It is **qualified rather than deleted**, because the paragraph it sits in is **C15's fix** and the *"read `own.speedMps`, not a velocity component"* anchor must survive; only the false universal goes, followed by the one case where it does not hold. **Both are corrections of false statements about the shipped system and NEITHER is recorded as a remedy for C23**, which is held in Tier 1 by clauses 7 and 8 and depends on the model reading nothing. **Coupled pins moved with the text:** doctrine **9,782 → 10,612** bytes and prefix **11,600 → 12,430**, in `tests/PromptRendererTests.cpp`. **The direction is the safe one for the third time** — the prefix GREW, so the cached block moves further above Haiku 4.5's 4,096-token minimum rather than toward it, and the token figures are **derived from the byte delta and the measured 3.955 B/token, not measured**: no hosted request was made and no grant was spent.

    **(h) What this revision does not do.** It does not quote a new acceptance or latency figure — the probe issues no orders, so the sentinel is untouched. **It does not claim the settling behaviour is understood**: why an aircraft under a commanded 300 settles near 140, and why it stops at exactly 1.5000, are both inside a closed-source engine and are recorded as observations rather than explained. And **it does not close C23 outright.** What is left is not engineering: the owner's view on the five judgement calls in `docs/c23-report.md` §7.3, and whether clause 8's acceptance criterion should name the run rather than the offline suite as its instrument. **162/162.** Running total unchanged at **≈$2.57 of $5**.

Here the model is running, talking, and behaving exactly as it always has.

In run 1 it held **320.0000 m/s for the entire 600 s under twenty accepted `hold` orders**; in run 2 it never went below **220.0**. **Zero samples below `safety.minSpeedMps` in either run, against 21 / 18 / 18 in the three runs before.** **The archive's below-floor total is still 58, and every one of the 58 predates the fix.**

Pooled in-engine acceptance moves **64.8 % [59.3, 70.0] → 71.1 % [66.4, 75.5]** over **398** resolved orders and 25 runs, and **82.0 % → 85.8 % [81.5, 89.3]** excluding the two non-model classes. The sentinel is regenerated by `tools/acceptance-report.py` and pinned across three documents. **No rate is claimed from two runs.** What one run may close is a mechanism readable off recorded values, and *"does the commanded aircraft still stop flying?"* is one: 0 below-floor samples against 57, and 0 `requestHoldPosition` calls against every hold.

    **(e) The commanded arm scored the archive's first ON-arm kill, and the qualification travels with the number rather than after it.** `RedSu35_02_wpn_1050_3` destroyed `BlueF16_02` at a **0.025 m** miss distance, `pk` 0.999997. **But `RedSAM_Launcher` had already taken that target to `wrecked` at `cumPk` 0.859** — which is precisely the qualification item 50(b) attached to the archive's first kill and item 51(g) to its second. **A kill by the engine's definition and by `analyse-outcomes.py`'s; not an unaided one.** **The better result in the same run is not a kill at all:** `RedSu35_01` took `BlueF16_01` from untouched to `wrecked` with **two of its own missiles and no SAM contribution** (`cumPk` 0.651 → 0.898). **This is the first time a commanded aircraft has done material damage on its own**, and it is reported as one observation, not as a capability.

    **(f) One earlier reading weakens, and it is this document's own.** The script-only arm returned **3 / 2 / 0 / 0 in both runs**, matching `095026` rather than the 2 / 2 / 1 / 0 of `135722` and `185750`. **That arm has now produced each result twice**, so item 51(g)'s *"the script-only arm carries no model and is close to deterministic … two matching runs of that arm are nearer to one observation than to two"* **does not hold as stated**, and `095026` is no longer *"the outlier that wants explaining"*. The variance is real and unexplained. **Nothing about what the commander is worth follows from that either**, and none is claimed.

And they say nothing about any model other than the shipped default. Running total unchanged at **≈$2.57 of $5**.

56. **The instrument behind a green metric has not compiled for eleven revisions and nothing in this project could have said so. Repairing it answered H3's open arm and refuted a hypothesis raised while repairing it.** *(v1.8.40, 2026-08-09.     **(a) `tests/live/` stopped compiling at v1.8.28 and nothing noticed.** C18 replaced `OrderSnapshot::headingDeg` with a derived `courseDeg`; `LiveMain.cpp` kept assigning the deleted field. **`ai-commander.slnx` contains exactly one project — `ai-commander.vcxproj` — and CI builds the plugin and the unit suite by explicit path and never touches `tests/live/`.** So the harness sat outside every build that runs. **It is the sole instrument behind the FIXTURE acceptance metric, which §Success metrics has read MET at 100 % since 2026-08-04.** **A metric whose instrument does not compile is a metric nobody can re-measure, and the verdict had been quoted for thirty-six revisions.**

    **(b) The corpus had diverged three times over, and one of the three still compiled — which is why it is the worst of them.** `speedMps` arrived at v1.8.25 (C15) and `courseDeg` at v1.8.28; **neither was ever set here**, so the fixture prompt lacked the two own-ship fields the doctrine tells the model to read for cruise speed and direction. `TrackReport` gained `kind` and `team` at v1.8.30, and the three-field aggregate initialisers **silently defaulted both to `Other`/`Unknown`** — reintroducing, in the measurement corpus alone, the precise ambiguity item 46(c) added those fields to remove. Repaired, with `speedMps` and `courseDeg` **computed by the plugin's own free functions** rather than typed, so a fixture cannot carry a speed and a velocity that disagree — which is C15 arriving in the instrument instead of the product.

    **(c) A hypothesis raised during the repair is REFUTED by the repair's own measurement, and it was this analysis's, made an hour before it was tested.** The reading was that the stale corpus *explained* C17 — that the fixture instrument scored 100 % partly because it fed the model an older, easier prompt. **Re-measured on the corrected corpus, with `own.speedMps`, `own.courseDeg` and populated `kind`/`team`, fixture acceptance is still 200/200 = 100 %.** **The divergence was real and it was not the explanation.** **C17's gap is what it always said it was: synthetic fixtures against real scenario state**, and this revision restores the MET verdict on a current instrument rather than overturning it. Recorded because a hypothesis that survived one hour before its own measurement refuted it is exactly what this section is a record of.

    **(d) H3's comparison arm ran for the first time, and H3 is fully validated by a wider margin than it claimed.** Two 200-order soaks, identical corpus and prefix, the `format` document the only difference — *"the same soak run twice"*, which is the instrument the row specified in v1.0 and never got. **Constrained: 200/200 accepted, `reject.schema` 0.00 %. Unconstrained: 0/200, `reject.schema` 100.00 %.** The hypothesis predicted *"double-digit rates from free-form prompting"*; the measurement is **100 %**, so it was conservative. **And the failure is one repeatable thing rather than a distribution: all 200 fail with `unknown top-level property 'rulesOfEngagement'`.** The model spells the ROE field in English prose instead of the schema's `roe`, **on every single attempt**. **That is a name, not a value, which is why the retry budget could never have rescued this arm** — a retry re-rolls a value and would have re-emitted the same field name 200 times. **`--no-format` is the standing control from here and it costs nothing to re-run.**

    **(e) C17's remaining item is specified** — see §Success metrics' new subsection. One test (*could a better order have been accepted from the same prompt?*), the two current members with their named defects, and three rules: no exclusion without a named mechanism, never publish the excluded figure alone, and **a frozen class must converge with the unexcluded figure or the fix did not work.** That last one is a live check rather than bookkeeping, and item 55 is the first revision to exercise it.

What belongs there is proof that the harness still compiles against the types it measures. **This is the same shape as item 50(e)'s finding and the opposite direction of travel from item 33's:** FR↔UAC parity is checked mechanically, spec↔code agreement is checked by nobody, and **instrument↔product agreement was checked by nobody until this revision.**

It does not re-run the hosted arm, which would need a grant. And **it does not close C17**: the taxonomy was C17's remaining *item*, not its question, and the two instruments still disagree by design. Running total unchanged at **≈$2.57 of $5**.

57. **The phased work is declared finished, the register empties for the first time, and what made a two-row backlog feel endless turns out to have been a missing close condition rather than a defect rate.** *(v1.8.41, owner decision 2026-08-09. **No run, no network, no cost, no grant, no code change, and no measured figure moves.** The options were drafted as a proposal first — `docs/phase-close-proposal.md`, retained and marked resolved — because writing either one into §Rollout would have *been* the decision, and §Scope authority says this document changes when a decision is made rather than when one is suggested.)*

    **(a) The diagnosis, because the remedy only makes sense against it.** Phase 3 closed at v1.8.17. Twenty-four revisions followed with **no phase, no gate and no close condition** — revisions that closed C5, C8, C11–C16, C18–C22 and C23's engineering, and that found the defect making commanded aircraft die. **None of that is in question. What was missing is a state the project could be in other than *"here is what is still open"*.** With no gate, the only status signal is the register, and **a defect register is never empty by construction**, so *"are we done?"* had no answerable form. **This is a documentation defect, and it produced the impression of an unending defect stream over a period in which severity was falling and the open count was two.**

    **(b) The reframe that does most of the work, stated because it is free and nobody had said it.** **§Corrections grows monotonically and is a HISTORY, not a backlog.** It is at 57 items and will only ever be longer. **The register is the backlog and it had two rows.** Reading the first as the second makes any project look like it is drowning, and this one especially — its corrections entries are long and written in the register's voice.

    **(c) C17 CLOSES as a stated position, on the precedent C8 set at v1.8.36 (closed on a decision, not on a measurement).** Its remaining *item* — the normative rejection taxonomy — landed in v1.8.40. Its *question* was answered by the owner on 2026-08-06: the bar stays on the fixtures. **What kept the row open is that the decision does not make the two instruments agree — which is a permanent condition and not a task**, and **a row nobody can ever action is exactly what v1.8.33's three-state fix was written to eliminate.** The caveat is not lost: it lives in §Success metrics beside the number, where a reader meets it, rather than in a register they may never open.

    **(d) C23 CLOSES on the mechanism, demonstrated under a commander, with its residual named rather than absorbed.** Clauses 7 and 8 are implemented and pinned by six offline tests of which **three fail against the pre-fix script**; the onset is gone across two three-arm runs; and **the model's behaviour was held constant and proven constant — 52 of 52 measurable holds still ordered at 0.00 m — so the only variable that moved is Tier 1.** **What does NOT close: clause 8 has never fired in a commanded scenario**, because clause 7 keeps preventing the onset, so the safety net's evidence is the offline suite plus one injected probe. **A net that has never caught anything in production is not thereby proven.** Under (f)'s entry rule an untested path is not a defect and does not open a row; it is recorded in the close, and the row **reopens if any run puts an entity below `safety.minSpeedMps` for more than one cadence window.**

    **(e) Every row now carries a KIND — `product` or `instrument` — and the split was worth making because it restores a signal that was there all along.** The last five revisions found, in order: an aircraft that stops flying (**product**), a recovery threshold sitting inside the band a recovering aircraft settles in (**product**), a measurement harness that had not compiled for eleven revisions (**instrument**), a fixture corpus three revisions stale (**instrument**). **That is a falling severity curve and it was invisible while both kinds queued together** — a reader counting open rows saw four problems where there were two and diminishing. **An `instrument` row is not a lesser obligation** and item 56 is the record of what leaving one costs; what the label buys is that a reader can tell whether a finding can reach somebody running a scenario.

    **(f) The entry rule tightens, because this register is now the only tracker.** A row SHALL be opened only for **a defect with a named mechanism** or **a decision with a named decider** — a person, not a phase and not a date. Everything else goes to §Out of scope as a DEFERRED row with a revisit condition, the instrument v1.8.33 built for precisely this. **A register row for *"we should measure this someday"* is invisible debt wearing a tracker's clothes**, which is OQ-4's failure mode and item 49(a)'s subject. **The discipline that used to come from a phase gate has to come from the entry rule now, and that substitution is the whole risk of this revision.**

    **(g) One requirement is corrected on the way past, and it is the same class of defect as items 52(f) and 56.** AIC-ORD-2's clause 8 acceptance criterion read *"recovers above it within one cadence window … asserted in the offline Lua suite"* — but **the suite observes the verbs a script issues and has no aircraft to watch accelerate.** The wording is **split rather than softened**: the suite asserts the **command**, and `tools/run-c23-probe.ps1` asserts the **recovery**, measured at **1.5000 m/s to above the floor in 3.1 s at +20 m/s²** on both aircraft (item 54(d)). **Two instruments, each asserting what it can see, and both named** — which is the discipline C17 exists to enforce and which this criterion had been quietly breaking since it was written.

    **(h) What this revision gives up, and it is a real cost rather than a rhetorical one.** **Maintenance forecloses the outcome question.** What the commander is *worth* now stands permanently at **unmeasured**: the first unconfounded comparison was a null at n = 1 (item 47(b)), the repeat refuted the identity without replacing it (item 50(a)), and the two post-fix runs give intervals that overlap almost entirely. **Anyone later asking "is this worth deploying?" gets no answer from this document, and that is now a property of it rather than a gap someone is closing.** The runs cost ~35 minutes and no grant; **reopening the question needs only an owner who wants it.** The alternative — Phase 4 — was declined because its three substantive deliverables need a reviewer, repeats nobody has committed to, and a documentation split, **and a gate whose pass condition depends on appetite that may not exist is the failure item 49(a) already names.**

    **(i) What maintenance does not mean.** The code is not frozen — defects get fixed. No bar moves: the gates that pass today are the gates that must pass tomorrow. Nothing here re-verdicts a metric, and the hosted latency row still reads MISSED. And **the standing hosted-egress authorization is still outstanding and is deliberately not made a register row**: it lives in §Review checklist, where it has a home and an owner, and duplicating it here would be double-tracking a decision that is already tracked. Running total unchanged at **≈$2.57 of $5**.

58. **The outcome question is reopened by the owner, and the planning analysis finds that the instrument built to answer it cannot.** *(v1.8.42, owner decision 2026-08-09.)* **No run, no network, no cost, no grant, no code change and no measured figure moves.** This item is a pre-registration; everything in it is written **before** the campaign it specifies.

    **(a) The close named its own reopening condition and the condition was met.** §Rollout's maintenance close said what the commander is *worth* stands at **unmeasured**, and that reopening the question *"needs only an owner who wants it and ~35 minutes a run"*. **The owner wants it.** **Maintenance is not rescinded** — no phase opens, no gate is created, the register stays empty and its entry rule is untouched, and no bar moves. **A close that can be reopened by a named decider is the kind this document was trying to write.** The alternative, a close nobody could reopen, is the failure mode item 49(a) already records under a different name.

    **(b) THE CENTRAL FINDING, AND IT ARRIVED BEFORE ANY RUN DID: THE FOUR COLUMNS THIS PROJECT MEASURES OUTCOMES WITH CANNOT ANSWER THIS QUESTION AT ANY n ANYONE WILL RUN.** `tools/analyse-outcomes.py` reports launches, detonations, kills and losses. Re-derived over the five archived three-arm runs as **paired ON − SCRIPT-ONLY** differences — the arm pair that moves only the commander — the runs needed for 80 % power are **launches 17, detonations 42, kills 140**, against a campaign anyone would actually run. **The instrument was built in v1.8.30 to close the gap item 45 opened, and it closed a different one:** it made outcomes *visible*, which was the point and was worth it, and it never had the resolution to make them *comparable*.

    **(c) And `losses` — this document's starkest figure — has been degenerate since the reference-script fix.** It read **26 commanded aircraft destroyed against 0** across the pre-fix pairs, which is the number §Summary still leads with and the number that justified C21. **In all three arms of all five three-arm runs since the fix it is identically 0.** A column with no variance discriminates nothing; a reader who checks it sees nothing and concludes, wrongly, that there is nothing there. **The defect it detected was fixed so thoroughly that the detector went blind**, which is a good outcome for the product and a silent one for the instrument, and nothing in this document would have said so.

    **(d) The signal did not disappear — it went into a field the instrument thresholds away.** Every `Warhead damage applied` line the engine writes carries a graded `pk`, and the kills column asks only whether `state=destroyed`. **Damage absorbed by the commanded pair gives a paired difference of −0.683 with sd 0.203 — d = 3.37, n = 3 for 80 % power.** Damage *dealt* gives d = 0.23 and n = 156, so the two halves of "combat outcome" are not equally reachable and only one of them is reachable at all. **The run logs have carried `pk` on every damage line since Phase 1b and no instrument this project owns has ever read it.** That is item 45's shape — *"the instrument already existed; nobody had run it"* — one turn worse, because here the instrument did not exist and the data sat under it for the whole of the project.

    **(e) The design is CONFIRMATORY and the document says so, because the endpoint was chosen by looking.** `damageAbsorbed` was found by inspecting the archive, not specified in advance of it. **So the five planning runs are excluded from the test**, and the decision rule, the n, the minimum detectable effect and the null wording are all fixed in §Validation's pre-registration rather than settled once the numbers are visible. **This project has four recorded results that did not survive their own repeat — items 40, 42, 47(b) and 50(a) — and in every one the analysis was chosen after the data.**

    **(f) Two limits are pre-registered rather than discovered in the write-up.** At the owner's chosen **n = 4**, a sign test **cannot reach α = 0.05 at all** — 4 of 4 consistent signs is p = 0.125 — so the paired *t* interval is the test and sign consistency is corroboration and not a second test. And because damage *dealt* is underpowered, **the campaign cannot separate "the commander makes the aircraft safer" from "the commander makes it fight less"**, whichever way the primary endpoint falls. **Both limits are properties of the design and are true before the campaign runs**, which is the only time it is honest to write them down.

    **(g) The corroborating mechanism is not a rate, and is reported beside the endpoint rather than merged into it.** Blue fires exactly **two** air-to-air munitions at the commanded pair in **15 of 15** archived arm-runs, so the denominator is a property of the scenario rather than a sample. **In the control arms both land: 20 of 20 munitions over 10 arm-runs.** In the commanded arm one is defeated in **4 of 5 runs**, and the engine names the mechanism instead of leaving it to be inferred — `[seeker] BlueF16_02_wpn_1250_4 lost`, **a line that appears in 0 of 10 control arm-runs**. Under §Scope authority rule 4 that is the one category a single run may close. **Conflating it with the rate is what item 40 records**, so it is quoted separately and never pooled.

    **(h) What this item does NOT do.** It reports **no outcome result**, because none has been measured under this protocol. It moves **no** §Success metrics verdict, quotes no new acceptance or latency figure, and leaves the sentinel untouched. It opens **no register row**: under §Maintenance's entry rule a measurement someone intends to take is not a defect and not a decision, and *"we should measure this someday"* is the invisible debt that rule exists to refuse. **The protocol is a specification in §Validation, where a reader looking for how a number was produced will find it.** Running total unchanged at **≈$2.57 of $5**.

59. **Clause 8's third instrument is specified: the one that exercises it in a commanded scenario, which nothing has ever done.** *(v1.8.43.)* **No run, no network, no cost, no grant, and no code — specified here first, per §Scope authority.**

    **(a) The gap is the one v1.8.41 recorded rather than carried, and it is worth restating exactly.** Across the two post-fix three-arm runs, **`navigation.requestHoldPosition` was called zero times and clause 8 never fired once** — clause 7 took all 33 `hold` orders and prevented the onset. **That is the designed relationship between the two clauses and not a defect in either.** It is also the reason clause 8's entire evidence is **the offline suite, which has no aircraft, plus one probe run with the commander asserted OFF.** **A safety net that has never caught anything with the product running is not thereby proven**, and item 57(d) said so at the close instead of pretending otherwise.

    **(b) More scenario repeats cannot close it, and the argument is item 51(f)'s, one clause downstream.** Clause 8 sits **below** clause 7. In this scenario nothing else stalls an aircraft, so **clause 7 working correctly is precisely what keeps clause 8 unexercised — and every further run makes that more true rather than less.** Item 51(f) reached the same wall for the distant hold: *"the counter-instance this row wanted cannot be obtained by running more scenarios … it must be injected."* **The remedy is the same remedy, and `tools/c23-hold-probe.lua` is the precedent for how to build it.**

    **(c) The instrument is the shipped script plus an injector, and that distinction is the whole design.** `tools/c8-floor-probe.lua` is **`lua/ai_commander_interceptor.lua` unmodified** — clauses 7 and 8 are the shipped code rather than a re-implementation, which is what `c23-hold-probe.lua` could not claim because it was a bare instrument that implemented no AIC-ORD-2 row at all. Onto that it adds a **time-boxed injector** calling `navigation.requestHoldPosition` at the aircraft's own position — **the one call clause 7 forbids** — bypassing `flyHold` to reproduce the archived degenerate hold. **The injector stops the instant ground speed falls below the floor, and everything after that point is the shipped clause 8 acting alone**, with the commander ON and orders flowing.

    **(d) What it proves, and what it deliberately does not, written before it runs.** It proves clause 8 **fires, takes navigation, and returns the aircraft above `safety.minSpeedMps` within one cadence window while a live commander is publishing orders** — the assertion neither existing instrument makes. **It does NOT prove that any ordinary order path reaches clause 8.** No such path is known in this scenario; the probe does not invent one and does not imply one. **The stall is injected, and every quotation of this result SHALL say so** — the same discipline item 54 applied to the distant hold, which was also a state the model would never produce.

    **(e) The criterion is extended, not rewritten, on v1.8.41's own precedent.** That revision split clause 8's criterion across two instruments because the offline suite cannot watch an aircraft accelerate. This adds a third for the axis neither covers — **a live commander in the loop.** **Three instruments, each asserting what it can see, and all three named**, which is what C17 exists to enforce.

    **(f) What this does not do.** `lua/ai_commander_interceptor.lua` is untouched and no behaviour changes. No bar moves and no §Success metrics verdict moves. **It opens no register row:** under §Maintenance's entry rule an untested path is not a defect, and this is the instrument for a residual the close already named rather than a new finding. Running total unchanged at **≈$2.57 of $5**.

60. **The last unticked box of this project's own gets a draft in front of the owner — and drafting it found that a standing grant currently has nothing to stand on.** *(v1.8.44.)* **No run, no network, no cost, and NO GRANT.** The draft **authorizes nothing**, the §Review checklist box **stays unticked**, and **no hosted request may be made under it.**

    **(a) The box was asking for a KIND of permission and not an AMOUNT of one, which is why six grants did not add up to it.** All six — v1.8.1, v1.8.3, v1.8.5, v1.8.8, v1.8.11, v1.8.19 — **authorize measurement**, each says so in its own text, each is scoped to named experiments with a derived cost and a cap, and **v1.8.19 states that a later grant does not inherit an earlier one's boundary.** So nothing authorizes running the hosted backend **as a product** — for someone operating a scenario rather than measuring one. **That box has been correctly unticked for its whole life, and v1.8.21 was right to separate it from the one above it.**

    **(b) THE FINDING, AND IT IS THE REASON THIS ITEM IS NOT JUST PAPERWORK: THERE IS NO SPEND CEILING ANYWHERE IN THE SHIPPED CODE.** `CommanderConfig.h` carries `claude.enabled`, `claude.model`, `claude.maxTokens` and `claude.apiKeyEnvVar`. **There is no per-run, no per-day and no cumulative cost bound, and no counter that could enforce one.** The `$5` budget this document has tracked for forty revisions is **a convention maintained by hand in §Cost model, enforced by nothing.**

    **(c) Under six measurement grants that was safe, and the reason is worth naming because it is exactly what a standing grant removes.** Every hosted run this project has ever made was **individually authorized, individually costed and individually recorded** — so a **human checkpoint sat in front of every single request**. That checkpoint, and not any code path, has been the spend control. **A standing authorization removes it by design. So it has to put something in its place, and this is the first revision in a position to say what.**

    **(d) The exposure is derived rather than asserted.** `commander.cadenceS` (20 s) and `claude.maxTokens` (512) bound the request *rate* and the per-request *size*, so a run's cost is bounded by its length: at **≈$0.001223** per order and two commanded entities, one order each per cadence is **6 orders/min ≈ $0.44/hour**; a ten-minute smoke is **≈$0.073**. **What nothing bounds is the number of runs.** Against the **≈$2.43** remaining that is about **5.5 hours** of continuous two-entity commanding — **so a scenario left running overnight with the commander enabled exceeds this project's entire budget by roughly 2×, and no code path would notice.**

    **(e) The draft separates three decisions the box has always bundled, because bundling them is how a governance decision gets made by accident.** ① **The data boundary** — may real scenario state from an arbitrary deployed mission leave the machine *standingly*? **C1 released that boundary once, by explicit owner decision, for one named run.** ② **Standing versus per-run** — one authorization for an indefinite series, or a record per run? ③ **Who holds it** — the owner personally, or **anyone in possession of the release tree**, for whom `claude.enabled=true` in a deployed config would then be a sufficient authorization by itself. **Each has a different answer available and each can be refused without refusing the others.**

    **(f) Three conditions a "yes" would have to carry, each named against the failure it prevents.** ① **A cumulative ceiling enforced in code rather than in this document** — a counter, a configured ceiling, and a refusal that turns `claude.enabled` off rather than logging; **it does not exist and would have to be built.** ② **The transmitted-field list re-reviewed against the mission actually deployed**, because the enumerated list is a property of the snapshot builder while *which scenario's values fill it* is a property of whoever deploys. ③ **The repository-visibility answer travels with it** — those two boxes are **the same decision seen from two sides**, what may leave the machine, and answering one alone leaves the weaker governing.

    **(g) A decision to say NO would tick this box as completely as a decision to say yes.** The box asks for **a decision**, not for a permission, and *"the hosted path stays a measurement instrument and never ships"* is a complete answer to it. **What it cannot be is left implicit** — `claude.enabled` is one line in a config file, and the only thing standing between it and a live request is that nobody has written it.

    **(h) What this item does not do.** It changes **no default**: `commander.enabled` and `claude.enabled` stay `false` in the shipped config under every answer, and the Operational readiness boxes are untouched. It makes **no request** and spends **nothing**. It opens **no register row** — under §Maintenance's entry rule this is a decision with a named decider, and it already has a home in §Review checklist, where item 57(d) deliberately left it rather than double-tracking it. Running total unchanged at **≈$2.57 of $5**.

At **t=103.9 the SHIPPED SCRIPT logs *"RedSu35_02 below flying speed at 47.0000 m/s; Tier 1 takes navigation"*** — that line is emitted by `lua/ai_commander_interceptor.lua`, not by the probe, so **it is the product speaking.** The injector latches off on the same sample. **Above the floor again at t=104.5, 53.0000 m/s — 0.6 s against a 20 s cadence window.** The hysteresis latch clears at *"recovered to 101.0 m/s; navigation returns to the posture"*, and the aircraft accelerates to **320.0000 m/s at +20 m/s²** — **the exact mirror of the deceleration, and the same ±20 m/s² the v1.8.38 probe measured from the other end on two aircraft.**

    **(d) The reopen condition is not met, stated rather than left to inference.** C23 reopens if an entity is *"observed below `safety.minSpeedMps` for more than one cadence window in any run"*. **This entity was below it for 0.6 s of 20 — by the operation of the design under test.** **C23 stays closed**, and the row now carries this note so *"has never fired"* stops being quoted from it.

    **(e) A corroboration this run was not looking for, and it is the better half of the result.** The order accepted at **t=104.4 — mid-recovery — carries `cruiseSpeedMps = 121`.** That is **the universal speed echo of item 53(b) happening live, during a clause 8 recovery**: the snapshot caught the aircraft at ~121 m/s and the model handed it straight back as the ordered cruise speed. **Clause 8 ignored it, because the clause re-accelerates to Tier 1's own `kRecoverSpeedMps` and never to a speed read from an order** — which is the exact sentence the clause was written around and which had, until this run, only ever been argued from 61 archived orders. **Offered at that strength and no more:** at 121 m/s the aircraft was already above the floor, so this particular echo could not have re-stalled it. **What is demonstrated is the echo under recovery, not a re-stall averted.**

    **(g) WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW, and it travels with every quotation of it: that any ordinary order path reaches clause 8.** No such path is known in this scenario, because **clause 7 prevents every naturally occurring onset — which is the designed relationship and not a gap.** **THE STALL WAS INJECTED.** The probe does not imply a reachable path and the criterion does not claim one.

63. **The owner authorized hosted egress, and the first thing that authorization needs is the control it was drafted against.** *(v1.8.47.)* **No run, no network, no cost, no code — specified first, per §Scope authority — and NO REQUEST is made under the authorization by this revision.**

    **(a) The authorization, and why the box is not ticked yet.** The owner authorized hosted egress on **2026-08-09**, answering the §Review checklist box v1.8.44 drafted. **That draft named three conditions a standing grant would have to carry, and condition ① does not exist:** there is no spend ceiling anywhere in the shipped code. **A grant recorded against a control that does not exist is exactly the paperwork this document spent forty revisions learning not to write** — it would read as governance and function as nothing. **So the ceiling is built first and the grant is recorded in the next revision, naming it.** The authorization is not in doubt; its enforcement is being supplied before it is written down.

    **(b) The defect this exposed is real and old, and it is opened as C24.** Under six *measurement* grants the absence of a ceiling was safe **for a reason that is about to stop being true**: every hosted run was individually authorized, costed and recorded, so **a human checkpoint sat in front of every request this project has ever made.** A standing authorization removes precisely that checkpoint — which is its purpose. **The defect did not appear today; the control that masked it is what is going away.**

    **(c) The ceiling latches, and that is not a detail.** The adapter maintains a cumulative cost for the life of the process and, on reaching `claude.maxSpendUsd`, **stops sending for the life of the process** and logs the exhaustion once. **A ceiling that is re-checked but not latched spends one more request every cadence, forever** — at a 20 s cadence that is 180 requests an hour past a limit it reports having reached.

    **(d) IT FAILS CLOSED, and this is the design decision worth arguing.** A value at or below zero **disables the hosted backend** rather than meaning "unlimited". The opposite convention is the more natural one to write, it is what most configuration does, and **it is the wrong one here: the failure mode of an unset, mis-parsed or zeroed field must be *sends nothing*.** The natural convention makes a typo into unbounded egress. Default **1.00 USD**, ≈ 2.3 hours of two-entity commanding at the measured per-order cost.

    **(e) The unit prices are configuration and not constants, and item 54(e) is why.** `claude.model` is operator-settable, so **a price compiled into the adapter is a number nothing keeps in step with the model it prices** — the identical shape to the doctrine block that stated a rejection threshold as *"at or below zero"* while the shipped bound had been 50.0 for nine revisions. Four fields, and the cost of a response is computed over the four token counts AIC-BE-2 has already recorded since v1.8.18.

    **(f) The refusal reaches the existing ladder rather than a new path.** It surfaces as a **transport failure whose detail names the budget**, so reject-and-retain handles it exactly as it handles an outage. **No new reject reason** — the taxonomy is normative under C17 and a budget stop is not a model failure. **And no silent stop:** a commander that quietly ceases to command is indistinguishable from one whose backend is down, and that ambiguity is what the detail string exists to remove.

    **(g) WHAT IT DOES NOT BOUND, stated rather than left to be assumed. It is PER-PROCESS.** It bounds **any single engine session** — which is the exposure item 60(d) actually derived, *"a scenario left running overnight"* — and it does **not** bound running the engine a hundred times. **That is deliberate and is not a gap being excused: starting a run is a human act, and the per-run human checkpoint is the control that covers repetition.** A cross-process ceiling would need durable state this plugin has no home for, and inventing one would put a spend counter in a file an operator can delete — **a control that can be reset by deleting a file is worse than none, because it reads as a control.** Running total unchanged at **≈$2.57 of $5**.

## Problem statement

> **When** an operator wants an entity in a running N8RO scenario to behave adaptively — to change posture, re-prioritize targets, or break off — **they must** hand-author that judgment ahead of time as a deterministic Lua ladder, **which means** every scenario's tactical repertoire is frozen at authoring time and every new situation requires a scripting change by someone who knows both the tactics and the Lua API.

The tree ships 6.5 GB of quantized language models (`data/ai/model/`), a doctrine corpus (`data/ai/context/`), an MCP stack, and a documented `n8ro-llm` module — and no working path from any of it to entity behavior in a running scenario. Meanwhile `oppint_red_interceptor.lua` demonstrates how good the deterministic layer already is: two-ship target deconfliction, launch-range discipline at 0.8 of kinematic reach, shoot-look-shoot with a flight-time-derived assessment window, 40° crank geometry, defensive pump inside 15 km, winchester egress. Its 455 lines encode real judgment. What they cannot encode is *situational* judgment — the script's posture ladder at lines 346–439 (`defend` → `rtb` → `ingress` → `crank` → `engage`) is a fixed priority cascade, and changing it means editing Lua.

The commander's job is to replace exactly that cascade — the posture selection — with model-issued intent, and to leave the flying logic alone.

### Prior art and lessons learned

- **`n8ro-llm` was designed for this space and does not solve it.** `docs/modules/n8ro-llm/` describes a `SimLuaLLMHost` with a 7-step RAG pipeline on message-bus topics `n8ro-llm/generate` and `n8ro-llm/generate/result`. There is no `n8ro-llm.dll`, no import library, and no headers under `include/`. Beyond being absent, its pipeline generates *Lua scripts* — an authoring aid, not a control path. What we learn: the useful seam is a message-bus request/response boundary, and this plugin should be structured so it can adopt that boundary later without redesign (see OQ-3).
- **The MCP stack exists and does not control entities.** *(v1.4 — verified; OQ-4 resolved.)* `bin/ai/run-full-stack.cmd` brings up `n8ro-data-bot.exe` → `n8ro-sim-bot.exe` → `bin/ai/n8ro-mcp.exe` over ZMQ IPC. The sim bot registers exactly two tools — `workbook_describe_api` and `workbook_eval` — and the data bot's ~37 tools are all database-authoring operations that never touch a running scenario. What we learn: the tree's existing AI surface is built for *authoring* (edit the scenario) and *interactive debugging* (eval Lua against a running sim), and nobody has yet built the third thing — a bounded, autonomous, per-entity control path. That is the gap this PRD fills, and it is a gap by design rather than by omission: `workbook_eval` deliberately gates mutation behind human approval, which is the right answer for a debugging tool and the wrong shape for a 20-second cadence.
- **The Lua sandbox closes the obvious shortcut.** The scripting sandbox opens only `base`, `math`, `table`, `string`; `os`, `io`, `package`, `require`, `load`, and `dofile` are explicitly disabled, and every hook runs under a Lua instruction budget. There is no pure-Lua route to an HTTP call or an async wait. Whatever does the inference must be C++.
- **What is different this time:** the LLM is scoped out of the control loop from the first line of design, rather than being retrofitted out after a latency measurement disappoints.

## Goals and success metrics

### Goals

1. **An entity in a running scenario changes posture on model-issued intent, with no change to platform binaries.** Measured by: a live scenario run in which posture transitions in the entity's log correspond to accepted orders.
2. **The simulation update thread never waits on inference.** Measured by: per-frame plugin cost histogram (below).
3. **No invalid, hallucinated, or unsafe order ever reaches a `request*` verb.** Measured by: the validator's rejection counters plus an adversarial unit-test corpus.
4. **A run is reproducible from its order log.** Measured by: the replay determinism test.
5. **The hosted-API path is off unless an owner turns it on, and what it transmits is enumerated and asserted.** Measured by: default config state plus the transmitted-field allowlist test.

***(v1.8.30 — the outcome row, and why it is `report, don't bar`.)*** For six metrics and twenty-nine revisions this table contained **no outcome measure at all**, and the gap is not merely that outcome went unmeasured: **the metric set above is satisfiable in full by a system that does harm.** Every published verdict was green or explained while the commanded aircraft were being destroyed in 22 of 24 runs (§Corrections items 45 and 46). That is the strongest available argument for the row, and it was already in hand.

The footing follows **v1.7.5's precedent and for the same reason.** That precedent was set when the in-engine acceptance n was 10 and a bar would have fired on noise; the outcome n is worse — twelve pairs, one scenario, one force laydown. **A bar on kills would bar a quantity that is zero in both arms, and a bar on losses would fail every run**, and both would train readers to ignore the row, which is exactly the failure v1.7.5 was avoiding.

Three properties of the row are load-bearing. **Four columns, not one** — item 45(d) had to correct a *"hits"* column that counted detonations, and a single conflated number would reintroduce it. **The row states its own confound**: the control arm swaps the shipped mission script **and** disables the commander, so a reader who takes it as a commander A/B has been misled; once C22's script-only arm exists the row carries three arms. **And the baseline is populated rather than `N/A`** — every other row in this table was written before there was anything to put in it, and §Corrections is largely a record of what that cost.

The target is left unchanged because meeting it is exactly the question OQ-8 asks, and moving a target to match a measurement would erase the signal.

#### The acceptance row is measured by two instruments that disagree, and this document has only ever gated one *(v1.8.25 — opens C17)*

**Both numbers below are honest and neither is wrong. They are not two estimates of one quantity.**

| Instrument | What it measures | n | Result | Gated? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **200-order soak** | The full pipeline against the six **synthetic `LiveMain` fixtures** — invented values in a real snapshot's field set. **The fixtures do not merely have easier inputs; they have inputs this document wrote** | 200 (local), 240 (hosted) | **100 %** | **Yes — ≥ 95 %, and the row above reads `MET (fixtures)`** |
| **Paired live runs** | The same pipeline inside the engine against **real scenario state** from a deployed mission | **109 resolved** post-fix, 12 pairs, 2 models *(v1.8.30)* | **79.8 % [71.1, 86.9]** pooled post-fix (87 of 109); **74.2 % [67.8, 79.9]** over the whole archive (158 of 213) | **No — reported only** |

***(v1.8.30 — the in-engine figure below was one run stale, the verdict cell is now qualified at the point of the verdict, and one contaminant in the instrument is named for the first time.)*** Three changes, none of which moves a verdict.

**The figure was superseded by this project's own next run.** Run `20260807T133621Z` was archived after §Corrections item 45 was written and nobody folded it in. Recomputed over the full archive: **7B post-fix is 59/70 = 84.3 % [73.6, 91.9]**, not 50/58 = 86.2 %; **14B post-fix agrees exactly at 28/39 = 71.8 % [55.1, 85.0]**; pooled post-fix is **87/109 = 79.8 % [71.1, 86.9]**. The intervals are computed with an implementation validated against this section's own published *"roughly [75 %, 93 %]"* for 50/58. **The direction is unchanged and no bar is newly met or missed** — the point is that a headline number in §Success metrics went stale under a subsection describing why it needed watching, **which is the same class of staleness C17 is about.**

**The verdict cell above now names its instrument.** `MET` unqualified could be, and was, quoted out of the context that qualifies it — a reader looking up *"did acceptance pass?"* reads the table, and the two-instrument discussion is nine lines and one heading further down. **A qualified verdict cannot be quoted unqualified**, and that is a one-cell change rather than more prose. Prose was tried across two revisions and this section's own number went stale underneath it. **The owner's 2026-08-06 decision is preserved intact: the bar stays on the fixtures.** What changes is that the fixture instrument is named where the verdict is.

**And a contaminant in the in-engine instrument, never previously named.** Of 55 archived rejections, **10 (18.2 %) are `roster` — *"entity 'RedSu35_0X' no longer exists"*, orders that resolved after the aircraft they were for had been destroyed.** They are not model failures in any sense. Excluding them moves whole-archive acceptance from 74.2 % to **77.8 %**. **The coupling is the interesting part: `roster` rejections can only occur when commanded aircraft die, and commanded aircraft die because of C21** — so the in-engine acceptance rate, the number this row is a dispute about, is **partly a function of the Tier-1 defect C21 names**, and that component will partly disappear when C21 is fixed. The two instruments disagree for one more reason than item 41 lists, and it is a reason with a fix already specified.

**In-engine acceptance SHALL be quoted as an interval, not as a point estimate** *(v1.8.30)*. Every interval in play is 15–30 points wide; a bare decimal to one place implies a precision the sample does not carry, and it is the form in which 86.2 % survived its own successor run.

***(v1.8.36 — the rule above was written in v1.8.30 and the figure went stale twice more while it stood. A rule that depends on a person remembering it is not a control, so the number now has an owner and a pin.)*** **`tools/acceptance-report.py` owns the in-engine figure.** It recomputes it over every `*/orders.jsonl` in the archive, refuses to print anything until its interval implementation reproduces this section's own published **50/58 → [74.6 %, 93.9 %]**, and emits a sentinel line. **`tools/lint-prd.ps1` fails the build when the PRD, the summary and the README do not carry the identical sentinel**, which is the same mechanism that has kept the summary's version stamp from drifting since v1.8.30 — the one control in this project that has never failed. It **cannot** recompute the figure itself: the archive lives outside the repository by design and the linter must run on a bare checkout. So the split is deliberate — **the tool owns the number, the linter owns the agreement**, and a refresh is a three-line paste.

<!-- in-engine-acceptance: 80.8 [77.4, 83.8] n=609 runs=30 -->

**And the census is the argument for fixing defects rather than moving bars.** Of **115** archived rejections, **58 (50.4 %) are the C23 stall floor** — an aircraft parked at 1.5 m/s, the snapshot reporting it honestly, the model copying it faithfully — and **10 (8.7 %) are `roster`**, orders that resolved after their aircraft was destroyed. **Neither class is a model failure.** Excluding both moves the figure from **71.1 % [66.4, 75.5]** to **85.8 % [81.5, 89.3]**. **Half of this metric's shortfall was one defect**, which is why C17's remedy was C23's fix and not an adjustment to the bar. *(A split for reading, not a normative taxonomy — that is specified before it is relied on.)*

***(v1.8.39 — the prediction in the sentence above was tested and it held.)*** C23's fix landed and two three-arm runs followed. **The stall-floor class did not grow: it is still 58, and every one of those 58 samples predates the fix.** The two post-fix runs contributed **74 resolved orders and one rejection** — a `track`, not the floor — so the pooled figure moved **64.8 % [59.3, 70.0] → 71.1 % [66.4, 75.5]** on 74 orders. **The count of 58 is now frozen rather than merely current**, and its share of rejections will fall with every further run; a reader seeing 50.4 % should read it as *"half of every rejection this project ever recorded came from one defect that no longer occurs"* rather than as a live proportion.

***(v1.8.26 — the in-engine instrument has been re-measured after C15 and C16, and the result strengthens this row rather than settling it.)*** Three further 7B pairs on the fixed build give **50/58 = 86.2 %**, against a pre-fix 7B baseline between **66.7 %** and **74.7 %** (§Corrections item 42(g) — item 40's 7B row names no runs and four subsets reproduce its figure). At n = 58 the 95 % Clopper–Pearson interval is roughly **[75 %, 93 %]**: it **excludes the ≥ 95 % bar** and **straddles the ≥ 90 % live-smoke assertion**, so no bar is established as met. **And the same runs supply the sharpest argument yet for this row.** §Corrections item 42(c) shows that part of the gain is a failure **changing category rather than disappearing**: the model still copies a velocity component into `cruiseSpeedMps`, but the copied value is now always positive, so what used to be **rejected and counted** is now **accepted and flown**. **An acceptance rate rose while the behaviour it stands in for did not improve** — which is precisely what a proxy metric measured on the wrong instrument does, and it happened on this project's own fix. The 14B arm did not run (**C20**), so C16's fix remains unmeasured in the engine.

**Why only one is gated, and the reasoning is v1.7.5's and is quoted rather than paraphrased.** The live-smoke gate was re-specified to *"**report** acceptance rather than bar it — the ≥ 95 % bar stays where the sample size is, on the 200-order soak."* At the time the in-engine sample was **10 orders** and the argument was sound: a rate over ten samples cannot separate a regression from bad luck, and a bar that fires on noise trains its readers to ignore it.

**What has changed is the n, and the argument has not moved with it.** Ten has become **54**, across seven pairs and two models, and at 54 a pooled rate is no longer noise — the 95 % Clopper–Pearson interval on 33/54 is roughly **[47 %, 74 %]**, which excludes both the ≥ 90 % live-smoke assertion and the ≥ 95 % soak bar by a wide margin. **The reason the bar sits on the fixtures is now a historical one rather than a statistical one**, and a rule kept past the condition that justified it is exactly what §Corrections is a record of.

**Why the two instruments disagree is partly known and partly not.** §Corrections item 41 establishes that **7 of the 12 rejections** in the four 14B pairs were C15 and C16 — this document's own defects, invisible on fixtures because a synthetic fixture has no spawn geometry to copy a velocity component out of and no model verbose enough to overrun a cap. That is a real answer and it is not the whole answer: three further rejections name already-detonated munition ids, one is B9 working as designed, and one is a genuinely destroyed entity. **The fixtures do not merely have easier inputs; they have inputs this document wrote**, which is the property that makes 100 % on them a weaker claim than its number suggests.

##### The rejection taxonomy, specified before it is relied on *(v1.8.40 — C17's remaining item)*

**Three documents quote an "excluding the two non-model-failure classes" figure, and until now the split behind it was a reading aid nobody had ratified.** §Corrections item 52(e) said so explicitly and deferred the specification. This is it.

**A rejection class is NOT a model failure if, and only if, the order it rejected could not have been made acceptable by the model reasoning better about the situation it was shown.** That is the whole test, and it is deliberately about the *order*, not about blame: it asks whether a perfect commander, given the identical prompt, could have produced an accepted order.

| Class | Test | Verdict | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`c23-stall-floor`** — `clamp` whose detail names `safety.minSpeedMps` | Could a better order have been accepted? | **NOT a model failure** | The aircraft was doing 1.5 m/s; the snapshot reported 1.5 m/s honestly; the doctrine told the model to start from the speed the aircraft is making. **Every legal answer above the floor contradicts the prompt the model was given.** The defect was Tier 1's and is fixed (C23) |
| **`roster`** — the entity was destroyed before the order resolved | Same | **NOT a model failure** | The order was already unexecutable when it arrived. **No content could have saved it**, and the class can only occur when commanded aircraft die |
| Every other class — `shape`, `range`, `track`, `fratricide`, `targetClass`, `transport`, and `clamp` on any other bound | Same | **Model or transport failure, counted in full** | A better order was available from the same prompt. `transport` is a host failure rather than a model one and is **still counted**, because excluding it would flatter the pipeline this metric measures |

**Three rules that stop this becoming a bin for inconvenient rejections.**

1. **A class may be excluded only after the defect that produces it is named in this document with a mechanism.** Both current members qualify: C23 and C21. **A class with no named defect behind it is a model failure by default.**
2. **The excluded figure SHALL NEVER be published alone.** It is quoted beside the unexcluded one, both as intervals, or not at all. `tools/acceptance-report.py` enforces this by printing both and neither separately.
3. **A class whose defect is fixed is FROZEN, not deleted.** Its historical count stays in the census and stops growing, so the excluded figure converges on the unexcluded one as the archive fills. **If the two ever stop converging after a fix, the fix did not work** — which is a live check rather than a bookkeeping convention, and v1.8.39 is the first revision to exercise it.

**What this does and does not settle.** It makes the 85.8 % figure quotable, and it gives the census a rule a later reader can apply to a class this document has not seen. **It does not make the two instruments agree, and nothing here is intended to** — that is C17's standing position and the owner's 2026-08-06 decision is untouched.

**No verdict is changed here.** The MET above stands on the instrument it was measured with, and the in-engine figure stands beside it rather than replacing it. **Whether the ≥ 95 % bar moves onto the engine is an owner decision**, and it has a real cost either way: gating on the engine makes the metric answerable only by a ~22-minute paired run, and leaving it on the fixtures keeps a green row that the product does not reproduce against real state. Carried as **C17** so the tension is owned rather than resolved by whichever number is quoted first.

### Non-goals / deferred scope

- **Not a real-time LLM control loop.** The measured floor is 3–6 s per order for the 3B on CPU and 10–15 s for the 7B. Anything reactive — missile defeat, merge maneuvering, launch timing — stays in Tier 0/1 where it already works. The trade-off accepted: the commander cannot respond to events faster than its cadence, so Tier 1 must be able to act correctly on a stale order.
- **Not a replacement for deterministic tactics.** The commander parameterizes `oppint_red_interceptor.lua`'s behavior; it does not reimplement crank geometry, launch discipline, or defensive pump. The trade-off: order expressiveness is capped at what the existing verbs accept, which is precisely the point.
- **Not a scenario-authoring tool.** Generating scenarios, entity profiles, or Lua scripts is out. That is the space `n8ro-llm` was designed for, and it can have it.
- **Not multi-entity coordination in v1.** Orders are per-entity. Section-level intent ("two-ship pincer") is a genuinely different problem — it needs a shared world model, order consistency across entities, and conflict resolution. Deferred with a dated entry below.
